Italian food and drink brands.Heinz: Heinz is American, from Pittsburgh, and its ketchup bottle once carried the slogan '57 varieties', which wasn't an actual count.
Italian food and drink brands.Cadbury: Cadbury is British, founded in Birmingham in 1824 by a Quaker family who saw cocoa as an alternative to alcohol.

Italian food and drink brands.Kellogg's: Kellogg's is American, born in Battle Creek, Michigan, where corn flakes were first made as a health food.
Italian food and drink brands.Heineken: Heineken is Dutch, and its green bottle and red star are among the world's most recognized beer branding.

Middle Eastern dishes.Hummus: The word means 'chickpeas' in Arabic; the dip is ancient and tahini gives it a creamy richness.
Middle Eastern dishes.Falafel: Fried chickpea or fava bean balls; the word possibly comes from an Arabic word for 'pepper', and some say they began in Egypt.
Middle Eastern dishes.Shawarma: Meat stacked on a rotating spit and sliced thin; the name comes from the Turkish word for 'turning'.
Middle Eastern dishes.Tabbouleh: A Levantine salad where parsley, not bulgur, is the main ingredient, finely chopped with mint, tomato and lemon.
Middle Eastern dishes.Baba ganoush: A smoky aubergine dip, whose name is sometimes translated as 'pampered father', with the aubergines charred over a flame.
Middle Eastern dishes.Fattoush: A salad of crisp vegetables and fried pita pieces seasoned with sumac, a way to use up stale bread.
Middle Eastern dishes.Kibbeh: A bulgur and minced meat shell filled with spiced meat and pine nuts, often described as the national dish of Lebanon and Syria.
Middle Eastern dishes.Manakish: Flatbread baked with za'atar and olive oil or cheese, a typical Levantine breakfast.
Middle Eastern dishes.Labneh: Strained yoghurt that is thick and tangy like soft cheese, drizzled with olive oil and used as a dip.
Middle Eastern dishes.Mujaddara: A humble dish of lentils and rice topped with crispy onions, and one of the oldest in the region, often called poor man's food.
Middle Eastern dishes.Kofta: Spiced minced meat shaped around skewers or into balls, found from Morocco to India under many names.
Middle Eastern dishes.Paella: A Spanish rice dish from Valencia, not Middle Eastern, but the Moors introduced rice to Spain.
Middle Eastern dishes.Gazpacho: Spanish chilled tomato soup, not Middle Eastern.
Middle Eastern dishes.Pierogi: Polish filled dumplings, not Middle Eastern.
Middle Eastern dishes.Tacos: Mexican, not Middle Eastern, though tacos al pastor were inspired by Lebanese shawarma.
Middle Eastern dishes.Ramen: Japanese noodle soup, not Middle Eastern.
Middle Eastern dishes.Pad thai: Thai stir-fried noodles, so it isn't Middle Eastern.
Middle Eastern dishes.Ceviche: A Peruvian dish of raw fish cured in citrus juice, not Middle Eastern.
Middle Eastern dishes.Goulash: A Hungarian stew flavoured with paprika, not Middle Eastern.
Middle Eastern dishes.Risotto: Italian rice cooked slowly with stock until creamy, not Middle Eastern.
Middle Eastern dishes.Borscht: A beetroot soup from Ukraine and Eastern Europe, so it isn't Middle Eastern.
Middle Eastern dishes.Poutine: A Canadian dish of fries, cheese curds and gravy, from Quebec.
Middle Eastern dishes.Pho: Vietnamese noodle soup, so not Middle Eastern.
Middle Eastern dishes.Ratatouille: A French Provençal vegetable stew, not Middle Eastern, though it is also made with aubergine.

Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Whisk: Whipping egg whites by hand can multiply their volume many times, and a copper bowl helps stabilize the foam.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Spatula: Its name comes from the Latin spatha for a broad, flat blade, the same root that gave us the word spade.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Ladle: The Big Dipper constellation is named after this tool in North America, since the stars trace its bowl and handle.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Tongs: One of humanity's oldest tools, it began as a pair of sticks or wooden tweezers to move hot things from fire.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Peeler: The swivel Y-peeler was invented in Switzerland in 1947, and the Rex peeler design it started with is still sold today.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Grater: A box grater has several surfaces, from fine zesting holes to coarse shredding, so one tool does four jobs.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Rolling pin: French-style tapered pins have no handles, which lets bakers feel the dough's thickness through their palms.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Colander: In 2011 an Austrian man won the right to wear one on his head in his driver's license photo as a Pastafarian.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Sieve: Sifting flour once removed bugs and grit. Modern flour is clean, so sifting now mostly aerates it.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Zester: The zest holds the citrus fruit's fragrant oils. The white pith under it is bitter, which is why you only take the colored layer.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Garlic press: Crushing garlic ruptures more cells than slicing, which releases more allicin and makes the flavor much sharper.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Potato masher: Unlike blenders, mashers don't overwork the starch, which can turn potatoes gluey. So it works better by hand.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Mortar and pestle: People have pounded spices in them since the Stone Age, and Thai curry pastes are still traditionally ground in granite ones.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Blender: Stephen Poplawski patented the first electric blender in 1922, originally to make soda fountain malted drinks.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Toaster: The pop-up toaster was patented in 1919 by Charles Strite, who wanted to end burned toast in his factory cafeteria.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Microwave: Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket near radar equipment in the 1940s, leading to its invention.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Dishwasher: Josephine Cochrane patented the first practical one in 1886, because she was tired of servants chipping her china.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Fridge: The compressor requires power. Einstein and Leo Szilard patented a design with no moving parts in 1930.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Stand mixer: KitchenAid's first model came out in 1919. It started as a heavy commercial machine for bakers before heading to homes.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Food processor: The home version arrived in the US in the 1970s via Cuisinart, adapted from a French restaurant machine.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Air fryer: It's basically a small, fast convection oven. Philips launched the first version in 2010.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Rice cooker: Toshiba launched the first automatic electric model in 1955 in Japan, and it needed an electric heating element.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Slow cooker: Crock-Pot launched in 1971 and was based on a bean-cooking appliance, but it still draws power.
Kitchen tools that don't need electricit.Bread maker: These became popular in Japan in the late 1980s, and they run on electricity to knead and bake.

Italian pasta sauces.Carbonara: Carbonara is the Roman pasta of eggs, cheese, guanciale and pepper; real versions contain no cream, which Italians view as heresy.
Italian pasta sauces.Bolognese: Bolognese, or ragù alla bolognese, is a slow-cooked meat sauce from Bologna, which is traditionally served with tagliatelle, not spaghetti.
Italian pasta sauces.Pesto: Pesto comes from Genoa and is named for the Italian 'pestare', to pound, since it was traditionally made in a mortar.
Italian pasta sauces.Arrabbiata: Arrabbiata means 'angry' in Italian, and the sauce is a tomato sauce fiery with red chili peppers.
Italian pasta sauces.Puttanesca: Puttanesca is a punchy sauce of tomatoes, olives, capers and anchovies, and its name roughly means 'in the style of a prostitute'.
Italian pasta sauces.Amatriciana: Amatriciana is a sauce from the town of Amatrice, made with guanciale, pecorino and tomato; it was a regional dish before spreading across Italy.
Italian pasta sauces.Cacio e pepe: Cacio e pepe means 'cheese and pepper', and the glossy sauce comes from only pecorino, black pepper and starchy pasta water.
Italian pasta sauces.Marinara: Marinara literally means 'mariner's style' in Italian, and the tomato sauce is a fast one, supposedly made by sailors.
Italian pasta sauces.Aglio e olio: Aglio e olio, 'garlic and oil', is a classic of Naples, and it's an easy late-night pasta of just garlic, olive oil and chili.
Italian pasta sauces.Alla Norma: Alla Norma is a Sicilian sauce of tomato, fried eggplant and ricotta salata, and it was named after Bellini's opera Norma.
Italian pasta sauces.Vongole: Vongole means clams in Italian, and spaghetti alle vongole is a Neapolitan dish served in a light garlic, wine and olive oil sauce.
Italian pasta sauces.Hollandaise: Hollandaise is a French butter sauce, whose name means 'Dutch', and it's an emulsion of egg yolks, butter and lemon.
Italian pasta sauces.Béarnaise: Béarnaise is a French sauce, a hollandaise with tarragon, and it's named after Béarn, the region of its supposed origin.
Italian pasta sauces.Teriyaki: Teriyaki is a Japanese glaze, so it isn't an Italian pasta sauce.
Italian pasta sauces.Sriracha: Sriracha is a Thai chili sauce, and it's not an Italian pasta sauce.
Italian pasta sauces.Tzatziki: Tzatziki is a Greek yogurt and cucumber sauce, often with garlic, and not Italian.
Italian pasta sauces.Chimichurri: Chimichurri is an Argentine herb sauce of parsley, garlic and vinegar, used on grilled meats and not on pasta.
Italian pasta sauces.Gravy: Gravy in the American sense is a meat-juice sauce, though some Italian-American families call their red sauce gravy.
Italian pasta sauces.Hoisin: Hoisin is a Chinese sweet bean sauce, and not an Italian pasta sauce.
Italian pasta sauces.Mole: Mole is a complex Mexican sauce of chilies and sometimes chocolate; some versions have more than 20 ingredients.
Italian pasta sauces.Satay: Satay sauce is a peanut sauce from Southeast Asia, so it's far from Italy.
Italian pasta sauces.Ranch: Ranch dressing was invented in California in the 1950s by Steve Henson, and it isn't an Italian pasta sauce.
Italian pasta sauces.Tahini: Tahini is a sesame paste from the Middle East, and not an Italian pasta sauce.
Italian pasta sauces.Romesco: Romesco is a Catalan sauce of roasted peppers and almonds, so it's Spanish, not Italian.

Islands in the Caribbean.Jamaica: Jamaica's Blue Mountain coffee grows high above Kingston and is one of the world's priciest.
Islands in the Caribbean.Hispaniola: Hispaniola is shared by Haiti and the Dominican Republic, and Columbus landed there in 1492.

Islands in the Caribbean.Dominica: Dominica is called the Nature Isle, and has the world's second-largest hot spring lake, the Boiling Lake.
Islands in the Caribbean.Antigua: Antigua is said to have a beach for every day of the year, and Nelson's Dockyard is a former Royal Navy base.
Islands in the Caribbean.Aruba: Aruba sits outside the hurricane belt, just off Venezuela, and is part of the Kingdom of the Netherlands.
Islands in the Caribbean.Curaçao: The blue liqueur takes its name from this Dutch island, where it was made with the peel of a local bitter orange.
Islands in the Caribbean.Puerto Rico: Puerto Rico is a US territory, and its Arecibo telescope was among the largest in the world until it collapsed in 2020.
Islands in the Caribbean.Martinique: Martinique is a French island where Mount Pelée erupted in 1902, destroying the city of Saint-Pierre.
Islands in the Caribbean.Guadeloupe: Shaped like a butterfly, Guadeloupe is an overseas region of France, so it uses the euro.
Islands in the Caribbean.Bermuda: Bermuda sits in the Atlantic about 1,000 km off North Carolina, far from the Caribbean despite its tropical image.
Islands in the Caribbean.Fiji: Fiji is in the South Pacific, a world away, with hundreds of islands and a famous bottled water.
Islands in the Caribbean.Maldives: The Maldives are in the Indian Ocean, and the lowest-lying country on Earth, averaging about 1.5 meters above sea level.
Islands in the Caribbean.Seychelles: The Seychelles are in the Indian Ocean, and the home of the giant coco de mer, the largest seed in the world.
Islands in the Caribbean.Mauritius: Mauritius is in the Indian Ocean and was once home to the dodo, which was extinct within about a century of discovery.
Islands in the Caribbean.Malta: Malta is in the Mediterranean, and the Knights of St John fortified it in the 1500s.
Islands in the Caribbean.Canary Islands: The Canaries are in the Atlantic off Morocco, and are named not for birds but for dogs, from the Latin for dog.
Islands in the Caribbean.Azores: The Azores are in the mid-Atlantic, and are an autonomous Portuguese region, nearer to Europe than to the Caribbean.
Islands in the Caribbean.Tahiti: Tahiti is in the South Pacific, where Gauguin spent his later years painting.
Islands in the Caribbean.Zanzibar: Zanzibar lies off East Africa in the Indian Ocean and was a major spice and slave trading hub; Freddie Mercury was born there.
Islands in the Caribbean.Sri Lanka: Sri Lanka lies in the Indian Ocean and is known for tea, formerly called Ceylon.

Landmarks in Spain.Alhambra: This Granada palace-fortress of the Moorish rulers is covered in intricate geometric tilework and carved plaster, and Washington Irving wrote about it.
Landmarks in Spain.Park Güell: Gaudí's hillside park in Barcelona was meant as a housing estate, and is famous for its mosaic lizard and wavy tiled bench.
Landmarks in Spain.Prado: Madrid's great art museum holds masterpieces by Velázquez and Goya, including Las Meninas, and it opened in 1819.
Landmarks in Spain.Mezquita: Córdoba's Mosque-Cathedral has a forest of over 800 red-and-white arches, and a cathedral built right inside the mosque.
Landmarks in Spain.La Rambla: Barcelona's busy tree-lined boulevard runs about 1.2 kilometres from Plaça de Catalunya to the old port.
Landmarks in Spain.Camp Nou: FC Barcelona's stadium is Europe's largest, holding nearly 100,000 fans when fully open, and it's being rebuilt.
Landmarks in Spain.Montserrat: A jagged mountain near Barcelona whose name means serrated mountain, with a Benedictine monastery housing the Black Madonna.
Landmarks in Spain.Teide: Tenerife's volcano is Spain's highest peak at about 3,715 metres, and measured from the ocean floor it ranks among the world's tallest volcanoes.
Landmarks in Spain.Canary Islands: This Atlantic archipelago lies off Morocco yet belongs to Spain, and its name likely comes from the Latin for dogs, not from the birds.
Landmarks in Spain.Ibiza: This Balearic island is known for nightclubs, but its old walled town Dalt Vila is a UNESCO site, and it has quiet coves too.
Landmarks in Spain.Seville Cathedral: One of the largest Gothic cathedrals in the world, it holds the tomb of Christopher Columbus and a former minaret as a bell tower.
Landmarks in Spain.Belém Tower: A Lisbon fortress from the early 1500s, it marked the departure point for Portugal's explorers, and so isn't in Spain.
Landmarks in Spain.Sintra: A Portuguese hill town of fairytale palaces near Lisbon, loved by Lord Byron, it is in Portugal, not Spain.
Landmarks in Spain.Douro Valley: Portugal's terraced vineyards are the oldest officially demarcated wine region in the world, producing port.
Landmarks in Spain.Mont Saint-Michel: A French abbey on a tidal island in Normandy, where the sea can rush in quickly, so it belongs to France.
Landmarks in Spain.Lourdes: A French Pyrenean town where Catholics believe the Virgin Mary appeared in 1858, drawing millions of pilgrims.
Landmarks in Spain.Carcassonne: A fortified medieval city in southern France, with over 50 towers, that inspired a popular board game.
Landmarks in Spain.Pena Palace: A colourful Romanticist castle in Sintra, Portugal, perched on a hilltop in bright yellow and red.
Landmarks in Spain.Algarve: Portugal's southern coast has golden cliffs and sea caves, such as Benagil, while it's not in Spain.
Landmarks in Spain.Madeira: A Portuguese island in the Atlantic, famous for its fortified wine and its tobogganing wicker baskets.
Landmarks in Spain.Azores: A Portuguese Atlantic archipelago with crater lakes and whale watching, roughly midway between Lisbon and New York.
Landmarks in Spain.Porto: Portugal's second city gave port wine its name, and its bookshop Lello is rumoured to have inspired Harry Potter.
Landmarks in Spain.Biarritz: A French Basque Country resort on the Atlantic that became Europe's surf capital after the 1950s.

3D shapes (not flat ones).Sphere: A sphere encloses the most volume for its surface area, which is why soap bubbles and raindrops tend toward it.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Cube: A cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices. Its sides are all equal, which is why dice use it for fairness.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Cone: A cone is made by spinning a right triangle about one leg, and the ancient Greeks sliced cones to discover ellipses and parabolas.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Cylinder: A cylinder's volume is exactly three times a cone's with the same base and height, a result Archimedes proved.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Pyramid: A pyramid can have any polygon for a base. The Great Pyramid of Giza was the world's tallest building for about 3,800 years.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Prism: A prism has two identical ends joined by flat sides. A glass prism splits white light into a rainbow, which Newton demonstrated.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Torus: A torus is the doughnut shape. Topologically a mug and a doughnut are the same shape, since each has one hole.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Tetrahedron: A tetrahedron has four triangular faces, the fewest any solid can have, making it the simplest 3D polyhedron.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Octahedron: An octahedron has eight triangular faces; it's the shape of a typical diamond crystal and an eight-sided die.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Dodecahedron: A dodecahedron has twelve pentagon faces. Plato linked it with the cosmos, and a 12-sided die is built on it.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Cuboid: A cuboid is a box with rectangular faces; most bricks, books and shoeboxes are this shape.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Circle: A circle is flat, with no thickness, so it is 2D. Spin it, and you get a sphere or a disk, but alone it isn't solid.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Square: A square is flat, so it is 2D. Give it depth and it becomes a cube, whose six square faces make a solid.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Triangle: A triangle is flat. Four of them joined into a solid make a tetrahedron, which is the simplest 3D shape there is.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Rectangle: A rectangle is flat, a 2D shape. Add height and it becomes a cuboid, which is the shape of most boxes and bricks.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Hexagon: A hexagon is flat, but honeycomb cells use it because it tiles perfectly with the least wax.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Pentagon: A pentagon is flat, but twelve of them fold together into a dodecahedron, one of the five Platonic solids.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Rhombus: A rhombus is a flat diamond shape with four equal sides. Its 3D relatives would be rhombohedra.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Oval: An oval is a flat, egg-like curve, so it is 2D. Its solid cousin is the ovoid, like an actual egg.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Trapezoid: A trapezoid has only one pair of parallel sides, and it is a flat shape. Its 3D look would be a truncated pyramid.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Parallelogram: A parallelogram is flat, with two pairs of parallel sides. Give it depth and you would get a parallelepiped.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Octagon: An octagon is flat, but a stop sign uses it so drivers recognise it from behind, too.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Kite: A kite is a flat shape with two pairs of equal adjacent sides. The 3D version would be a different solid.
3D shapes (not flat ones).Ellipse: An ellipse is flat, a squashed circle, and each planet orbits the Sun in one, as Kepler discovered around 1609.

Roles played by Robin Williams.Dr. Dolittle: Rex Harrison (1967) and Eddie Murphy (1998) played him. Williams played several doctors, but not the one who talks to animals.
Roles played by Robin Williams.Mr. Bean: Rowan Atkinson's nearly silent British comic character, created for TV in 1990, not a Williams role.

Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.The Simpsons: Running since 1989, it is the longest-running American animated series and scripted primetime show, with well over 700 episodes.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Family Guy: Seth MacFarlane voices Peter, Stewie, Brian and Quagmire himself. Fox canceled the show, then revived it after strong DVD sales and reruns.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Futurama: Matt Groening's follow-up to The Simpsons has been canceled and revived several times, and its writers' room included real math and science PhDs.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.King of the Hill: Mike Judge and Greg Daniels set this show in the fictional Texas town of Arlen. It ended in 2010 and was revived in 2025.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Bob's Burgers: Loren Bouchard's show follows the Belcher family restaurant, where Bob's chalkboard burger-of-the-day puns are a running gag.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.American Dad!: From Seth MacFarlane, it follows CIA agent Stan Smith. It began on Fox, then moved to TBS in 2014.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.South Park: It started as crude paper cutouts by Trey Parker and Matt Stone, and now episodes are produced in about a week to keep jokes topical.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Rick and Morty: Co-creators Justin Roiland and Dan Harmon grew it from a crude Back to the Future parody short called The Real Animated Adventures of Doc and Mharti.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.BoJack Horseman: Netflix's tale of a washed-up sitcom horse ran six seasons, hiding an unusually frank look at depression behind its animal puns.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Archer: FX's spy spoof ran 14 seasons from 2009 to 2023, powered by running gags like 'phrasing' and 'danger zone'.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Daria: Daria Morgendorffer first appeared as a classmate on Beavis and Butt-Head, then got her own deadpan MTV spin-off that ran 1997 to 2002.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Bluey: This Australian pup show is made in Brisbane for preschoolers, yet parents love it for its honest, funny take on playful parenting.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Peppa Pig: This British preschool series keeps each episode to about five minutes, and kids rewatch them endlessly.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Arthur: The PBS aardvark show ran from 1996 to 2022, widely cited as the longest-running American children's animated series.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Doug: Doug Funnie narrates his awkward life through journal entries. Nickelodeon launched the show in 1991, and it later moved to Disney.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Rugrats: Rugrats launched in 1991 as one of Nickelodeon's first three Nicktoons, alongside Doug and The Ren and Stimpy Show.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Hey Arnold!: Craig Bartlett's show is set in the fictional city of Hillwood, and the 2017 TV movie The Jungle Movie finally resolved its parents storyline.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Recess: Disney's Recess spends most of its time on the Third Street School playground, where kids run a society by schoolyard rules.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Ben 10: Ben Tennyson's Omnitrix watch lets him turn into alien heroes. This toy-friendly premise grew into an enormous Cartoon Network franchise.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Phineas and Ferb: The Disney Channel hit is built on 104 days of summer vacation, a theme song in every episode, and Perry the Platypus.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Gravity Falls: Alex Hirsch's Disney show hid cryptic ciphers in every episode, and he ended it after two seasons by design, not cancellation.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.PAW Patrol: Spin Master's Canadian series spawned a huge toy line. Its pups report to ten-year-old Ryder and live in Adventure Bay.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Dora the Explorer: Dora asks viewers to answer in Spanish, making her a pioneer of interactive preschool TV, while her monkey Boots wears red boots.
Animated sitcoms aimed at adults.Bob the Builder: The British stop-motion series made 'Can we fix it?' a catchphrase, and Neil Morrissey voiced Bob in the UK version.

Rappers.Eminem: Marshall Mathers' Lose Yourself was the first rap song to win the Oscar for Best Original Song, in 2003.
Rappers.Jay-Z: Shawn Carter built Roc-A-Fella and a business empire, and Forbes called him hip hop's first billionaire.
Rappers.Drake: The Toronto star began as an actor on Degrassi, and he is among the most streamed artists in the world.
Rappers.Kanye West: He started out as a producer, famous for chopped, sped-up soul samples before he became a star rapper.
Rappers.Tupac: His All Eyez on Me was a double album, and he was shot in Las Vegas in 1996 at age 25.
Rappers.Snoop Dogg: His Doggystyle debut in 1993 was produced by Dr. Dre and sold millions, and his laid-back flow is instantly recognizable.
Rappers.Kendrick Lamar: His album DAMN. won the 2018 Pulitzer Prize for Music, the first win for a non-classical, non-jazz work.
Rappers.Nicki Minaj: Born in Port of Spain, Trinidad, she moved to New York as a child and became one of the best-known female rappers.
Rappers.50 Cent: He survived being shot nine times in 2000, and called his debut Get Rich or Die Tryin'.
Rappers.Dr. Dre: An N.W.A founder, and his headphone company Beats was sold to Apple for about three billion dollars.
The Brooklyn rapper's debut Ready to Die appeared in 1994, and he was killed in 1997 at age 24.
Rappers.Missy Elliott: In 2023 she became the first female rapper inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, famous for Get Ur Freak On.
Rappers.Lil Wayne: He started on Cash Money as a child, and his Tha Carter III sold a million copies in its first week.
Rappers.Cardi B: Her Bodak Yellow in 2017 was the first number one by a solo female rapper in nearly two decades.
Rappers.Beyoncé: The superstar is a pop and R&B titan, though she raps a bit on tracks, and Destiny's Child came before. Not a rapper.
Rappers.Rihanna: The Barbados-born singer topped charts with Umbrella and Diamonds, with a pop and R&B base rather than rap.
Rappers.Usher: The R&B star of Yeah! worked with rappers like Ludacris, so it is easy to confuse him, but he is a singer.
Rappers.Bruno Mars: A pop-funk star from Hawaii who sings and dances, with hits like Uptown Funk, not a rapper.
Rappers.The Weeknd: The Canadian R&B singer headlined the 2021 Super Bowl, and he sings in a falsetto, not rap.
Rappers.Justin Bieber: The pop star was discovered on YouTube, and he sings rather than raps, despite many rap collaborations.
Rappers.Ed Sheeran: A trap. He raps rapid-fire verses in songs like Lego House, but he is a folk-pop singer-songwriter.
Rappers.Alicia Keys: The pianist and R&B singer wrote Fallin', and collaborates with rappers, but she is not one herself.
Rappers.John Legend: The soul singer and pianist reached EGOT status in 2018, after winning an Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony.
Rappers.Prince: A funk-pop genius who played nearly every instrument on his debut album, and famed for Purple Rain, but not a rapper.

Types of classical composition.Symphony: Haydn wrote over 100 symphonies and is often called the father of the form, and Beethoven's Ninth added a choir.
Types of classical composition.Concerto: A concerto features a solo instrument against an orchestra, and the soloist traditionally plays a showy cadenza.
Types of classical composition.Sonata: The word means 'sounded', as opposed to 'cantata', which is sung; the sonata form shaped classical music for two centuries.
Types of classical composition.Opera: The first operas were written in Italy around 1600, and the word simply means 'works' in Latin.
Types of classical composition.Fugue: In a fugue, a short theme is imitated by successive voices, and Bach's 'Art of Fugue' is a famous demonstration.
Types of classical composition.Overture: An overture started as the orchestral opening of an opera, and later became a concert piece alone, as with Tchaikovsky's 1812.
Types of classical composition.Requiem: A requiem is a mass for the dead, and Mozart left his unfinished at his death in 1791.
Types of classical composition.Oratorio: An oratorio is like an opera without sets or costumes, and Handel's Messiah is the most famous example.
Types of classical composition.Minuet: The minuet was a stately French dance in three beats, and it often sat inside symphonies until Beethoven's scherzos replaced it.
Types of classical composition.Etude: Etude is French for study, and Chopin turned technical exercises for the piano into concert masterpieces.
Types of classical composition.Nocturne: The nocturne is a dreamy night piece, and the Irish composer John Field invented it before Chopin made it famous.
Types of classical composition.Rhapsody: A rhapsody is a free-form piece; Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue premiered in 1924 with the composer at the piano.
Types of classical composition.Serenade: A serenade was meant to be played outdoors in the evening, and Mozart's 'Eine kleine Nachtmusik' is one.
Types of classical composition.Cantata: A cantata is a work for voices with instruments, and Bach wrote over 200 for church use.
Types of classical composition.Haiku: Trap: the haiku is a Japanese poem of three short lines, a poetry form and not a musical one.
Types of classical composition.Sonnet: Trap: a sonnet is a 14-line poem, and it only sounds like a sonata.
Types of classical composition.Limerick: Trap: a limerick is a five-line comic verse, named after a city in Ireland.
Types of classical composition.Novel: Trap: a novel is a long work of prose fiction, not a piece of music.
Types of classical composition.Sitcom: Trap: a sitcom is a TV comedy, not a classical composition.
Types of classical composition.Fresco: Trap: a fresco is a painting made on wet plaster, like Michelangelo's Sistine ceiling.
Types of classical composition.Sculpture: Trap: sculpture is three-dimensional art, not music.
Types of classical composition.Mosaic: Trap: a mosaic is an image built of small tiles, and has no musical form.
Types of classical composition.Essay: Trap: an essay is a short prose piece, and the word comes from the French for 'attempt'.
Types of classical composition.Fable: Trap: a fable is a short tale with a moral, like Aesop's, not a musical type.

Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Penalty spot: The penalty spot is 12 yards (11 metres) from the goal line, and the goalkeeper must stay on the line until the kick is taken.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Centre circle: The centre circle has a 10-yard radius, which is the distance opponents must keep from the ball at kick-off.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Goal line: The goal line is where the posts stand, and the whole ball must cross it entirely for a goal to count.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Touchline: Touchlines are the long sides, the boundaries that, when crossed, bring a throw-in; in some sports they're called sidelines.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Corner flag: Corner flags must be at least 1.5 metres tall, and a flag is placed at each of the pitch's four corners.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Halfway line: The halfway line divides the pitch into two equal halves, and players must stay in their own half at kick-off.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Penalty area: The penalty area is 18 yards from the goal line, where the keeper can use hands and fouls give a penalty.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Six-yard box: The six-yard box is the small box in front of goal, the spot for goal kicks, and it is smaller than the penalty area.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Goalposts: Goalposts on a full-size pitch are 8 yards apart, 7.32 metres, and 8 feet high.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Crossbar: The crossbar is the top of the goal, and the goal height is 8 feet (2.44 metres) tall.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Penalty arc: The penalty arc is the D-shaped curve outside the penalty area, which keeps players 10 yards from the spot.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Pitcher's mound: The pitcher's mound is the raised dirt hill in baseball, 60 feet 6 inches from home plate.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Home plate: Home plate is baseball's five-sided plate, the place where a run is scored.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.End zone: The end zone is American football's scoring area at each end of the field, 10 yards deep.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Free-throw line: The free-throw line is in basketball, 15 feet from the backboard, where shots are taken after a foul.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Crease: The crease is the goalie's area in ice hockey, and in cricket the line where the batter stands.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Blue line: The blue line in ice hockey marks the offside zone, and a puck carrier must cross it onside, or play is stopped; there are two on the rink.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Fairway: The fairway is the closely mown grass between the tee and the green in golf.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Tee box: The tee box is the starting area for each golf hole.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Baseline: The baseline is the end boundary of a tennis or basketball court, not a soccer pitch feature.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Service line: The service line is a tennis court line that marks where serves must land.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Faceoff circle: The faceoff circle is an ice hockey marking where play is restarted by a puck drop.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Three-point line: The three-point line is basketball's arc beyond which shots count for three.
Markings and features of a soccer pitch.Wicket: The wicket is cricket's set of three stumps, with bails across the top.

Decathlon events.100m: The decathlon's opening event; its winner is often called the fastest all-rounder, though the title of World's Greatest Athlete goes to the overall champion.
Decathlon events.Long jump: Decathletes get three attempts here, not six, and a single foul can wreck a score that took ten events to build.
Decathlon events.Shot put: The decathlon shot weighs 7.26 kg, about 16 pounds, the same as in the men's single event.
Decathlon events.High jump: Fosbury's backward flop, introduced at the 1968 Olympics, is now how nearly every jumper clears the bar, decathletes included.
Decathlon events.400m: Closing day one, this lap of the track is a notorious energy drain; many decathletes dread it more than the 1500m.
Decathlon events.110m hurdles: Decathlon hurdles are the same 106.7 cm height as in the specialist race, and knocking them over does not add a penalty.
Decathlon events.Discus: The men's discus is a 2 kg disc; throwers spin about one and a half turns to build speed before release.
Decathlon events.Pole vault: Often the decathlon's most dramatic event: vaulters pick their starting height and can fail three times, scoring nothing.
Decathlon events.Javelin: The javelin is 2.6 to 2.7 m long, and its centre of gravity was moved in 1986 to stop throws landing flat and dangerously far.
Decathlon events.1500m: The decathlon's final event, run when everyone is exhausted; the gap between athletes here is often a few seconds for the whole medal.
Decathlon events.Hammer throw: A trap: it is a field event, but not in the decathlon. The 7.26 kg ball on a wire appears only in the single-event programme.
Decathlon events.Triple jump: Not part of the decathlon, though it is also a jumping event. The decathlon limits jumps to long and high plus the pole vault.
Decathlon events.200m: Heptathletes run it, but decathletes do not; their sprint events are the 100m and 400m.
Decathlon events.800m: The women's heptathlon ends with this race, but the decathlon's finale is the longer 1500m.
Decathlon events.Marathon: At 42.195 km it is far beyond decathlon length; the decathlon's longest run is 1500m, under four percent of that distance.
Decathlon events.Steeplechase: A 3000m race with barriers and a water jump; it is part of the track and field programme but never the decathlon.
Decathlon events.Swimming: The modern pentathlon, not the decathlon, includes swimming, along with fencing, riding, shooting and running.
Decathlon events.Cycling: Triathletes and track cyclists use it, but decathlon, despite having ten events, has no bike leg.
Decathlon events.Fencing: One of the five modern pentathlon events, along with swimming, riding, shooting and running, not the decathlon.
Decathlon events.Archery: The decathlon is all running, jumping and throwing; aiming is not tested.
Decathlon events.Shooting: Shooting appears in the modern pentathlon and biathlon, but decathletes only throw things, never fire them.
Decathlon events.Equestrian: Show jumping is part of the modern pentathlon; the decathlon is purely about the athlete's own body.
Decathlon events.5000m: A distance-runner's event; the decathlon's longest race is just 1500m, so no one needs to run 12 laps.
Decathlon events.60m: A sprint held indoors; it appears in the indoor heptathlon, while the outdoor decathlon begins with the 100m.

Cycling races.Tour de France: The most famous of cycling's three-week Grand Tours; the race has run since 1903, and its leader wears the yellow jersey.
Cycling races.Giro d'Italia: Italy's Grand Tour, with a pink jersey for the leader because the organising newspaper was printed on pink paper.
Cycling races.Vuelta a Espana: Spain's three-week Grand Tour is the youngest of the big three, and its leader wears red since 2010, after previously wearing gold.
Cycling races.Paris-Roubaix: Nicknamed the Hell of the North, it covers rough cobbled farm tracks, and the winner gets a cobblestone as a trophy.
Cycling races.Milan-San Remo: At nearly 300 km, it is the longest one-day pro race, and is called La Primavera as it arrives at the start of spring.
Cycling races.Tour of Flanders: A Belgian classic of short, steep cobbled climbs, held each spring, and fans there consider the race a national passion.
Cycling races.Liege-Bastogne-Liege: The oldest Classic, from 1892, nicknamed La Doyenne, and it is a hilly route through the Ardennes.
Cycling races.Tour Down Under: The first big race of the pro season takes place in South Australia in January, under summer heat.
Cycling races.Il Lombardia: Known as the Race of the Falling Leaves because it comes in autumn, it is the last of cycling's five Monuments of the season.
Cycling races.Monaco Grand Prix: A motor race, with Formula 1 cars squeezing through the narrow streets of Monte Carlo.
Cycling races.24 Hours of Le Mans: A car endurance race in France where teams of drivers take turns over a full day and night.
Cycling races.Dakar Rally: Cars, trucks and motorbikes cross deserts, so it is a motorsport, not cycling.
Cycling races.Kentucky Derby: A horse race at Churchill Downs, run in about two minutes in the first week of May.
Cycling races.Boston Marathon: A road race for runners, and it is the world's oldest annual marathon, first held in 1897.
Cycling races.Grand National: A horse steeplechase held at Aintree, known for tall fences and many falls.
Cycling races.Iditarod: The race is for sled dogs and their mushers across Alaska, not for bicycles.
Cycling races.Ironman: A triathlon includes a bike leg of 180 km, which makes it tempting, but it also involves swimming and running.
Cycling races.Isle of Man TT: A motorcycle race, so the bikes have engines, which is why it does not belong among pedal-powered events.
Cycling races.The Boat Race: The Oxford-Cambridge rowing race on the Thames, where the crews use oars.
Cycling races.Daytona 500: A stock car race in Florida, with engines roaring at nearly 200 mph.
Cycling races.London Marathon: A running race, whose route passes landmarks such as Tower Bridge and the Mall, and where many runners wear costumes.
Cycling races.Wimbledon: A tennis tournament played on grass; it has been going since 1877 and has a strict all-white dress code.
Cycling races.Ryder Cup: A golf team contest between the USA and Europe, held every two years.
Cycling races.Indy 500: A 500-mile car race around an oval in Indianapolis, where winners drink milk.

Paralympic sports.Boccia: Boccia is a precision ball game for athletes with severe disabilities, similar to bocce. It's been a Paralympic sport since 1984.
Paralympic sports.Goalball: Goalball is for blind and visually impaired athletes. Players wear blackout eyeshades and listen to a bell inside the ball.
Paralympic sports.Wheelchair rugby: Originally nicknamed murderball, wheelchair rugby is a full-contact sport and was devised in Canada in 1977.
Paralympic sports.Para athletics: Para athletics has events in running, jumping, throwing, and racing with prostheses or wheelchairs. It's the Paralympics' largest sport.
Paralympic sports.Sitting volleyball: Players sit with part of the body on the floor and the net is lower than in standing volleyball. It's played at a fast pace.
Paralympic sports.Para swimming: Swimmers compete in classes by ability, and the sport has been in the Paralympics since the first Games in 1960.
Paralympic sports.Blind football: Blind football is played with a ball that rattles, with sighted guides and goalkeepers. Spectators are asked to stay silent.
Paralympic sports.Wheelchair fencing: Wheelchair fencers are fixed to the floor with frames, so they fight with arm and torso agility.
Paralympic sports.Para powerlifting: Para powerlifting involves the bench press for athletes with lower limb impairments, and has run at the Games since 1984.
Paralympic sports.Wheelchair tennis: The ball may bounce twice in wheelchair tennis, and it's one of the sport's best-known Paralympic events.
Paralympic sports.Bocce: Bocce looks like boccia, but is a different lawn game for the general public, so it's not a Paralympic sport.
Paralympic sports.Netball: Netball isn't at the Paralympics, though some countries run disability netball programs.
Paralympic sports.Squash: Squash is not a Paralympic sport, though it joins the 2028 Olympics.
Paralympic sports.Cricket: Cricket has a blind form, but it isn't part of the Paralympic program.
Paralympic sports.Darts: Darts is not a Paralympic sport, even though it has strong disability leagues.
Paralympic sports.Polo: Polo isn't a Paralympic sport. The Paralympics do have para equestrian.
Paralympic sports.Lacrosse: Lacrosse isn't a Paralympic event, and made its Olympic return in 2028.
Paralympic sports.Water polo: Water polo is an Olympic sport since 1900, but it has no Paralympic version, since players must tread water without touching the bottom.
Paralympic sports.Gymnastics: Gymnastics is Olympic, but the Paralympics have no gymnastics program.
Paralympic sports.Baseball: Baseball has its Olympic stints but not a Paralympic program.
Paralympic sports.Handball: Handball is Olympic, but has no Paralympic version.
Paralympic sports.Racquetball: Racquetball isn't part of the Paralympics.
Paralympic sports.Surfing: Surfing is Olympic since 2020, but not Paralympic, though adaptive surfing has world championships.
Paralympic sports.Golf: Golf returned to the Olympics in 2016, but it isn't a Paralympic sport.

Funfair and arcade games.Whack-a-Mole: Players pound plastic moles that pop up from holes. The arcade classic was created in Japan in 1975, and its original name was Mogura Taiji.
Funfair and arcade games.Skee-Ball: Rolling balls up a ramp into scoring rings. It was invented in 1908 in Philadelphia, and its tickets are redeemed for prizes.
Funfair and arcade games.Claw machine: A crane grabs a prize with a claw that is often set to grip loosely on purpose. The payout depends on a program, not just skill.
Funfair and arcade games.Ring toss: Players throw rings over bottle necks or pegs. Carnival versions often use rings barely larger than the target, so winning is a feat.
Funfair and arcade games.Pinball: Silver balls bounced by flippers. Flippers arrived in 1947 with Gottlieb's Humpty Dumpty, which turned a game of luck into one of skill.
Funfair and arcade games.Air hockey: A puck floats on a cushion of air blown through tiny holes in the table. It was invented in the 1960s by engineers at Brunswick.
Funfair and arcade games.Coin pusher: A machine where a moving shelf nudges coins toward an edge. The thrill is watching a heap of coins teeter over a ledge.
Funfair and arcade games.High striker: A strongman game where a mallet swing sends a puck up a tower to ring a bell. It dates from the nineteenth century, when fairs held strength contests.
Funfair and arcade games.Hoop shot: An arcade basketball game with a short time limit and an automated scoreboard. Machines usually tilt the hoop to increase the challenge.
Funfair and arcade games.Hook a duck: A fairground game where small ducks float in a pool and players use a hook on a pole to lift them. It's a classic prize game at fairs.
Funfair and arcade games.Coconut shy: A British fair game where players throw balls to knock coconuts off stands. It dates to Victorian fairs, and the coconuts are set loosely.
Funfair and arcade games.Water gun race: Players squirt streams at a target to fill a balloon or push a clown's mouth open. It is a timeless carnival favorite, built for quick competition.
Funfair and arcade games.Croquet: A lawn game of hitting balls through hoops with mallets. It is played on grass at clubs and gardens, not at arcades.
Funfair and arcade games.Bridge: A trick-taking card game with bidding that's popular in clubs. It is a mind sport, not a funfair game.
Funfair and arcade games.Mahjong: A tile game born in China in the nineteenth century. It calls for four players and quiet concentration, not noisy fair stalls.
Funfair and arcade games.Chess: A strategy board game with a 1,500-year lineage. After 1997, computers have beaten the best humans, and no arcade shout is needed.
Funfair and arcade games.Polo: A team sport played on horseback with mallets. It dates back some 2,000 years to Persia, so it is hardly an arcade pastime.
Funfair and arcade games.Curling: A game of sliding stones on ice toward a target. It's an Olympic sport with Scottish origins, and quite different from funfair play.
Funfair and arcade games.Fencing: Swordplay with foils, epees or sabres. It is a refined Olympic sport and not a stall at the fair.
Funfair and arcade games.Rowing: A sport of propelling a boat with oars. It's an Olympic mainstay, played on water and not on an arcade floor.
Funfair and arcade games.Cricket: A bat-and-ball game popular across the Commonwealth. A Test match can last five days, which is long even for a patient fairgoer.
Funfair and arcade games.Sudoku: A number puzzle on a nine-by-nine grid, popularized in Japan in the 1980s. It is a pencil-and-paper game, not an arcade attraction.
Funfair and arcade games.Lacrosse: A team sport using sticks with netted pockets, with Native American origins. It is played on fields, not midways.
Funfair and arcade games.Rugby: A contact team sport with an oval ball that started at Rugby School in England. It belongs on a pitch, not a funfair.

Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Heracles: Known to Romans as Hercules, he was the strongest Greek hero. He completed twelve labors as penance for killing his own family in a fit of madness.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Achilles: Hero of the Iliad, nearly invulnerable except for his heel. The Achilles tendon is named after him.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Perseus: He beheaded Medusa using a polished shield as a mirror, then used her head to turn a sea monster to stone and rescue Andromeda.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Theseus: He killed the Minotaur in the Labyrinth of Crete, and found his way out with a thread given by Ariadne. He became king of Athens.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Jason: Leader of the Argonauts, he sailed in the ship Argo to fetch the Golden Fleece, and Medea's magic made it possible.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Odysseus: The cunning king of Ithaca who thought up the Trojan Horse, then took ten years to sail home. His journey is told in the Odyssey.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Bellerophon: He tamed the winged horse Pegasus and killed the fire-breathing Chimera, but was cast down when he tried to fly to Olympus.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Ajax: A huge warrior who fought at Troy and was second only to Achilles. A cleaning product later borrowed his name.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Atalanta: A swift huntress who joined the Calydonian Boar hunt and refused to marry anyone who couldn't beat her in a footrace.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Diomedes: A Greek king who fought at Troy and, with Athena's help, even wounded gods in battle, including Ares and Aphrodite.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Hector: A trap: he was Troy's greatest warrior, a prince of Troy and the one Achilles killed. He is on the Trojan side.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Paris: A Trojan prince whose abduction of Helen started the Trojan War. He is credited with shooting the arrow that killed Achilles.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Aeneas: A Trojan hero, son of Aphrodite, who escaped the burning city. Virgil's Aeneid makes him the ancestor of Rome.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Beowulf: A Geatish hero of Old English poetry from Scandinavia. He fights the monster Grendel, not Greek foes.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Gilgamesh: A Mesopotamian king, not Greek. The Epic of Gilgamesh, written on clay tablets, is among the oldest known stories in the world.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Thor: The Norse god of thunder, wielding the hammer Mjolnir. He belongs to a different mythology.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Medusa: A monster, not a hero, and the one Perseus beheaded. Her gaze turned onlookers to stone, and snakes grew from her head.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Minotaur: A bull-headed monster that Theseus killed, rather than a hero. It lived in a labyrinth and was fed on young Athenians.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Cyclops: A one-eyed giant, a monster and not a hero. Odysseus blinded Polyphemus to escape his cave.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Sigurd: A Norse dragon-slayer who killed Fafnir, the Völsunga saga's hero. His German twin is Siegfried.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Cuchulainn: The warrior-hero of Irish legend, famed for single-handedly defending Ulster. He's Celtic, not Greek.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.King Arthur: A legendary British king whose knights sat at a round table. His tales are medieval, not part of Greek myth.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Hydra: A many-headed water serpent, a monster and not a hero. When one head was cut off, two more grew back.
Greek (not Trojan) heroes of myth.Romulus: The legendary founder and first king of Rome, said to be raised by a she-wolf. He is Roman, not Greek.

Battles fought before the year 1500.Marathon: In 490 BC Athens beat a Persian invasion, and the long-distance race is named for a legendary runner.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Thermopylae: In 480 BC Leonidas and his 300 Spartans, with other Greeks, held a narrow pass against the Persians.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Cannae: In 216 BC Hannibal surrounded a much larger Roman army, a classic double envelopment studied ever since.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Actium: In 31 BC Octavian's fleet beat Antony and Cleopatra, and soon he became Augustus.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Salamis: In 480 BC the Greek fleet lured the Persian ships into narrow waters and crushed them.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Gaugamela: In 331 BC Alexander the Great beat a much larger army of Darius III and Persia's empire collapsed.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Hastings: William of Normandy won in 1066. The fight actually took place at Senlac Hill, a few miles from the town.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Agincourt: In 1415 English longbowmen beat a bigger French army in muddy ground, as Henry V's campaign peaked.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Bannockburn: In 1314 Robert the Bruce's Scots beat a bigger English army and secured their independence.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Crecy: In 1346 English longbows crushed French knights, an early lesson in how archers could beat cavalry.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Tours: In 732 Charles Martel halted an Umayyad advance into France, a clash often credited with shaping Europe's history.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Hattin: Saladin destroyed the Crusader army in 1187, opening the way to retaking Jerusalem.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Waterloo: Napoleon's final defeat took place in 1815, more than three centuries after 1500.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Trafalgar: Nelson's 1805 sea victory against the French and Spanish is far later than 1500, in the Napoleonic era.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Gettysburg: The 1863 American Civil War battle, which Lincoln marked with a famous address, is long after 1500.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Somme: A 1916 World War I battle in northern France, more than four centuries after 1500.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Verdun: This 1916 battle in France lasted about ten months and cost huge casualties, but it belongs to World War I.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Stalingrad: The 1942 to 1943 battle on the Volga, a World War II turning point, took place more than 400 years after 1500.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Little Bighorn: In 1876 Sioux and Cheyenne warriors beat Custer's cavalry in Montana, nearly 400 years after 1500.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Austerlitz: Napoleon's 1805 triumph over Russia and Austria, remembered as his masterpiece, far after 1500.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Yorktown: The 1781 siege that effectively ended the American Revolutionary War, nearly three centuries after 1500.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Culloden: The 1746 defeat of the Jacobites was the last pitched battle on British soil, over two centuries after 1500.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Lepanto: The 1571 naval battle between a Holy League fleet and the Ottomans came only 71 years too late.
Battles fought before the year 1500.Bunker Hill: A 1775 Revolutionary War fight near Boston, where colonists were famously told not to fire until they saw the whites of eyes.

Writing systems from the ancient world.Hieroglyphs: Egyptian picture-writing was only deciphered in 1822, when Champollion used the Rosetta Stone.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Cuneiform: Wedge-shaped marks pressed into clay began in Sumer around 3400 BC, among the oldest writing known.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Linear B: The script of Mycenaean Greece was deciphered in 1952 by an architect, Michael Ventris.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Linear A: The Minoan script of Crete remains undeciphered, so its language is still unknown.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Runes: Germanic peoples carved these angular letters, which suit wood and stone better than curves.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Ogham: An early Irish script of notches along the edge of a stone, like tally marks.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Maya glyphs: The Maya script combined word signs with syllables, and has been largely deciphered since the late 1900s.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Oracle bone script: China's oldest known writing was scratched on turtle shells and animal bones for divination, in the Shang dynasty.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Phoenician: This consonant-only alphabet was ancestor to the Greek, Latin, Hebrew and Arabic scripts.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Indus script: Found on seals of a civilization about 4,000 years old, it has never been deciphered.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Demotic: The everyday Egyptian script was the middle one on the Rosetta Stone, between hieroglyphs and Greek.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Emoji: They began in Japan in the late 1990s, far from the ancient world.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Morse code: Samuel Morse's 1830s to 1840s invention is modern, a dot-and-dash code for the telegraph.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Braille: Louis Braille perfected it in the 1820s as a teenager, so it belongs to modern times, not antiquity.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Shorthand: Rome's Tiro devised shorthand for Cicero, but it abbreviates existing writing, not a script of its own.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Binary code: Leibniz described binary arithmetic in the 1700s, and computers later made it central to modern life.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Semaphore: Flag signaling stems from the 1790s, when Claude Chappe built his telegraph towers in France.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Klingon: A Star Trek language invented in the 1980s, with its own alphabet, so it is thoroughly modern.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Esperanto: Created in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof as a neutral second language, so it is far from ancient.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Sign language: Natural languages of gesture, not a script. Written forms came much later.
Writing systems from the ancient world.QR code: Invented in Japan in 1994 to track car parts, the code is a modern invention.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Barcode: Patented in 1952 and first scanned on a pack of gum in an Ohio supermarket in 1974.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Tengwar: J. R. R. Tolkien's invented elvish script from the 1900s, so it is a fantasy and not an ancient one.
Writing systems from the ancient world.Hashtag: Twitter popularized it in 2007, so it is a very new way of marking text.

Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Rosetta Stone: Found in 1799, its decree in three scripts let Champollion decode hieroglyphs in 1822.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Bayeux Tapestry: Actually an embroidery about 70 meters long, it tells the story of the Norman Conquest of 1066.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Terracotta Army: Farmers digging a well near Xi'an in 1974 found thousands of clay soldiers, each with a unique face.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Sutton Hoo helmet: Found in an Anglo-Saxon ship burial in Suffolk in 1939, it was rebuilt from hundreds of fragments.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Dead Sea Scrolls: Found from 1947 by a Bedouin shepherd in caves near Qumran, they include the oldest known copies of Hebrew Bible books.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Lewis Chessmen: Carved from walrus ivory in the 12th century and found on Scotland's Isle of Lewis in 1831.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Venus de Milo: Found on the Greek island of Melos in 1820, the statue lost its arms, and it now stands in the Louvre.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Book of Kells: An illuminated Gospel book from around AD 800, kept at Trinity College Dublin.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Domesday Book: William the Conqueror's 1086 survey was called Domesday because, like Judgment Day, there was no appeal.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Code of Hammurabi: These Babylonian laws, carved on a basalt stele around 1754 BC and held in the Louvre, include 'an eye for an eye'.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Nebra sky disc: This bronze disc, about 3,600 years old with gold stars, is among the oldest known depictions of the cosmos.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Ishtar Gate: A blue glazed-brick Babylonian gateway, rebuilt in Berlin's Pergamon Museum.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Holy Grail: Legend, not artifact: no one has ever found it, and its tale was shaped by medieval romances.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Excalibur: Legend: no sword has been proven to be King Arthur's, and the idea comes from medieval stories.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).One Ring: Tolkien invented it for The Lord of the Rings, so no one will ever find it.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Philosopher's Stone: Alchemists sought it for centuries and never found it; the first Harry Potter book renamed it the Sorcerer's Stone in the US.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Necronomicon: H. P. Lovecraft invented this fictional book of the dead.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Golden Fleece: Greek myth tells of the ram's fleece that Jason sought; no artifact has been found.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Mjolnir: Thor's hammer is mythical, though real Viking hammer pendants have been found in graves.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Pandora's box: In the Greek myth it was a jar (pithos), and the 'box' is a translation error by Erasmus.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Aladdin's lamp: It was not in the original Arabian Nights, but was added by Antoine Galland in the 1700s.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Elder Wand: Rowling's Elder Wand is the most powerful of the Deathly Hallows, and in the story it passes to whoever defeats its owner.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Heart of the Ocean: The blue diamond necklace in the 1997 film Titanic is fictional.
Real artifacts (not legend or fiction).Golden Snitch: A fictional Quidditch ball from Harry Potter.

Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Lascaux paintings: Painted about 17,000 years ago, it was found in 1940 by teenagers who followed their dog into a cave.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Gobekli Tepe: This Turkish site, about 11,500 years old, has carved stone pillars that predate farming and pottery.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Otzi the Iceman: He died in the Alps around 5,300 years ago, was found in 1991 and carried an arrowhead in his shoulder.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Skara Brae: An Orkney village of about 5,000 years ago, with stone furniture, uncovered by a storm in 1850.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Newgrange: An Irish passage tomb about 5,200 years old, where the winter solstice sunrise lights the chamber.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Catalhoyuk: A Turkish settlement about 9,000 years old whose houses were entered through the roof.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Jericho's walls: Early stone walls and a tower at Jericho date to around 9000 BC, among the world's earliest.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Chauvet cave art: France's cave paintings, about 36,000 years old, were sealed by a rockfall until 1994.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Venus of Willendorf: Found in Austria in 1908, the limestone figurine is about 25,000 years old.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Cuneiform: Sumerians pressed wedge shapes into clay by about 3300 BC, long before the Great Pyramid.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.The wheel: Wheeled vehicles appeared around 3500 BC, yet Egyptians dragged pyramid stones on sledges.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Parthenon: Finished in 432 BC, about two millennia after the Great Pyramid.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Colosseum: Built in AD 80, so about 2,600 years after the pyramid.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Great Wall of China: Its famous Ming-era form dates to the 1400s, and early walls were from the 7th century BC at the earliest.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Terracotta Army: The clay army dates to about 210 BC, over 2,300 years after the Great Pyramid.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Machu Picchu: Built in the 1400s AD, making it nearly four thousand years younger than the pyramid.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Rosetta Stone: Carved in 196 BC, so about 2,300 years after the pyramid.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Tutankhamun: The boy king ruled around 1330 BC, about 1,200 years after the pyramid.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Cleopatra: She lived around 30 BC, about 2,500 years after the pyramid.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Hanging Gardens: If real, they were built around 600 BC, about 2,000 years later.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Ramses II: He reigned from about 1279 BC, more than 1,200 years after Giza.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Phoenician alphabet: The Phoenician alphabet appeared around 1050 BC, and it is the ancestor of Greek and Latin.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Petra: The Nabataeans flourished around 300 BC, over two thousand years later.
Older than the Great Pyramid of Giza.Mayan pyramids: The Maya built their first pyramids around 1000 BC, much later than Giza.

Crops native to the Americas.Potato: Domesticated in the Andes about 8,000 years ago, the Incas freeze-dried it as chuño.
Crops native to the Americas.Tomato: The name comes from the Aztec 'tomatl', and Europeans suspected it as a poisonous nightshade for generations.
Crops native to the Americas.Maize: Domesticated from wild teosinte in Mexico about 9,000 years ago, a grass with a few hard kernels.
Crops native to the Americas.Cacao: Maya and Aztecs used the beans as money and drank bitter chocolate, often with chili.
Crops native to the Americas.Vanilla: An orchid from Mexico, hand-pollinated in 1841 by Edmond Albius, a 12-year-old enslaved boy on Réunion.
Crops native to the Americas.Peanut: Not a true nut but a legume, it ripens underground.
Crops native to the Americas.Pumpkin: Native Americans grew pumpkins for thousands of years, planting them with corn and beans as the Three Sisters.
Crops native to the Americas.Chili pepper: Domesticated thousands of years ago in the Americas, it makes capsaicin, which deters mammals but not birds.
Crops native to the Americas.Avocado: The word comes from Nahuatl ahuacatl, and it was domesticated in Mesoamerica thousands of years ago.
Crops native to the Americas.Pineapple: Native to South America, Columbus met it in 1493 on Guadeloupe, and it became a symbol of hospitality.
Crops native to the Americas.Sunflower: Native Americans grew it in eastern North America before 2000 BC, and Spaniards carried it to Europe.
Crops native to the Americas.Squash: One of the earliest crops domesticated in the Americas, about 10,000 years ago.
Crops native to the Americas.Wheat: Wheat was domesticated in the Fertile Crescent about 10,000 years ago, and it reached the Americas only with Europeans.
Crops native to the Americas.Rice: Rice was domesticated in China about 9,000 years ago, and Asia, not the Americas, is its home.
Crops native to the Americas.Coffee: Coffee comes from Ethiopia, and the Americas only got it in the 1700s, yet Brazil now grows the most.
Crops native to the Americas.Sugar cane: Sugar cane comes from New Guinea, and Columbus brought it to the Caribbean on his second voyage in 1493.
Crops native to the Americas.Banana: Bananas come from Southeast Asia and New Guinea, and they reached the Americas after 1500 with the Spanish.
Crops native to the Americas.Orange: Sweet oranges are a hybrid born in southern China and Southeast Asia, and they reached the Americas with the Spanish.
Crops native to the Americas.Apple: Apples come from the Tian Shan mountains of Kazakhstan, and the Spanish and English settlers brought them to America.
Crops native to the Americas.Grapes: Grapes were domesticated in the Near East and Caucasus, and European settlers carried them across the Atlantic.
Crops native to the Americas.Onion: Onions come from Central Asia, and the Egyptians already ate them thousands of years ago.
Crops native to the Americas.Olive: Olives come from the Mediterranean, and Spanish missionaries planted them in California.
Crops native to the Americas.Carrot: Carrots come from Persia and Afghanistan, where the first cultivated ones were purple, not orange.
Crops native to the Americas.Black pepper: Black pepper comes from India's Malabar coast, the spice Columbus hoped to find when he sailed west.

Traded along the Silk Road.Silk: Chinese silk was the route's namesake, and China guarded the secret of its making for centuries before it finally leaked westward.
Traded along the Silk Road.Spices: Pepper, cinnamon and cloves from Asia were prized in Europe, and for centuries they could cost as much as precious goods.
Traded along the Silk Road.Tea: Chinese tea traveled overland to Central Asia, where it was pressed into hard bricks that were easier to carry and even used as money.
Traded along the Silk Road.Porcelain: Fine Chinese ceramic became so associated with its origin that Europeans simply called it 'china', and Europe couldn't make its own until the early 1700s.
Traded along the Silk Road.Jade: Prized in China, jade came largely from Khotan, an oasis city on the southern branch of the Silk Road in the Tarim Basin.
Traded along the Silk Road.Paper: Invented in China, it traveled west along the road, and the Arab world learned papermaking after a famous clash at Talas in AD 751.
Traded along the Silk Road.Horses: Han China prized the powerful horses of Central Asia's Ferghana valley, so much that it sent armies to get them.
Traded along the Silk Road.Glassware: Roman and Persian glass flowed east. Fine pieces ended up in Chinese and even Japanese treasuries, where some still survive.
Traded along the Silk Road.Gold: It moved both ways as payment, and Central Asian and Roman gold coins have been found far from where they were minted.
Traded along the Silk Road.Silver: Silver coins from Persia and Central Asia were the standard currency of the Silk Road, and many merchants used them to settle accounts.
Traded along the Silk Road.Ivory: Elephant tusks from India and Africa were carved into luxury goods, and trade in them moved along the Silk Road for centuries.
Traded along the Silk Road.Potatoes: Trap: native to the Andes and unknown in the Old World until the Spanish brought them from South America in the 1500s.
Traded along the Silk Road.Chocolate: Trap: cacao came from the Americas, so it reached Europe only after Columbus's era, long after the Silk Road's heyday.
Traded along the Silk Road.Tobacco: Trap: an American plant that Europeans met only after 1492, so no Silk Road caravan carried it in antiquity.
Traded along the Silk Road.Rubber: Trap: rubber trees came from the Americas. Europe saw the stuff only after contact with the New World.
Traded along the Silk Road.Maize: Trap: corn was domesticated in Mexico thousands of years ago and reached the Old World only after Columbus.
Traded along the Silk Road.Tomatoes: Trap: Italian cuisine feels tomato-based, but the fruit came from the Americas and reached Europe only in the 1500s.
Traded along the Silk Road.Vanilla: Trap: the orchid is from Mexico, and for centuries only Mesoamerica knew the secret of its cultivation.
Traded along the Silk Road.Petrol: Trap: gasoline fuels cars, which didn't exist. The petrol business began in the late 1800s.
Traded along the Silk Road.Plastic: Trap: the first synthetic plastic, Bakelite, was only invented in 1907, so none moved along the ancient road.
Traded along the Silk Road.Pineapples: Trap: native to South America, pineapples reached Europe after Columbus, and became a luxury in 17th-century England.
Traded along the Silk Road.Peanuts: Trap: peanuts originate in South America, so no ancient Silk Road traders were selling them.
Traded along the Silk Road.Chili peppers: Trap: they came from the Americas, and Asian cooks adopted them after the 1500s, so spicy Sichuan food is fairly recent.
Traded along the Silk Road.Coca-Cola: Trap: invented in 1886 in Atlanta by pharmacist John Pemberton, so a drink far too modern for the old caravans.

Things in a first aid kit.Bandage: Linen strips served as bandages on wounds and mummies alike in ancient Egypt.
Things in a first aid kit.Gauze: Gauze is said to be named for Gaza, where the thin, loosely woven fabric is believed to have originated.
Things in a first aid kit.Antiseptic wipes: Alcohol disinfects best at about 70 percent, not 100, since a little water helps it penetrate germs before it evaporates.
Things in a first aid kit.Tweezers: For a tick, grasp it close to the skin and pull straight up; twisting or squeezing can leave mouthparts in the bite.
Things in a first aid kit.Medical tape: Paper tape is gentler on skin, while zinc oxide cloth tape is stronger and hold dressings in place longer.
Things in a first aid kit.Disposable gloves: Nitrile gloves are widely favored since latex allergies are common, and they hold up well against many chemicals.
Things in a first aid kit.Instant cold pack: Squeezing breaks an inner pouch so a salt such as ammonium nitrate dissolves in water, which absorbs heat and chills the pack.
Things in a first aid kit.Plasters: Earle Dickson invented the Band-Aid in 1920 for his clumsy wife, who kept cutting her fingers while cooking.
Things in a first aid kit.Burn gel: Cool running water for ten minutes or more is the first step for a burn; gel supplements, not replaces, that.
Things in a first aid kit.Sling: A triangular bandage becomes a sling in seconds, and the same cloth can do many other jobs.
Things in a first aid kit.Safety pins: They secure bandages and slings, a use almost as old as the pin's 1849 patent.
Things in a first aid kit.Fork: A fork has no medical use; it reached England in the 1600s and spread slowly, since people thought it silly.
Things in a first aid kit.Candle: A candle belongs in a power-outage kit, not on a wound, though old remedies did use wax and fat.
Things in a first aid kit.Lipstick: Lipstick isn't first aid, though lip balm sometimes appears in outdoor survival kits.
Things in a first aid kit.Stapler: Surgical staplers close wounds in hospitals, but an office stapler never belongs in a home kit.
Things in a first aid kit.Hairbrush: A brush doesn't treat injuries; first aid kits stick to dressings, tools and medicine.
Things in a first aid kit.Spatula: Wooden tongue depressors are basically small spatulas, yet a kitchen spatula isn't medical gear.
Things in a first aid kit.Lightbulb: A flashlight might sit in a kit; a bare bulb is useless on its own.
Things in a first aid kit.Toothpaste: Dabbing toothpaste on a burn is a persistent myth that can irritate skin and trap heat.
Things in a first aid kit.Paper clips: Paper clips are stationery; kits use safety pins to hold bandages instead.
Things in a first aid kit.Perfume: Perfume is cosmetic, and its alcohol would sting an open wound rather than help it.
Things in a first aid kit.Glitter: Glitter is decorative; microplastic glitter even worries environmental researchers.
Things in a first aid kit.Chopsticks: In a pinch a chopstick can splint a finger, but it isn't something a standard kit packs.
Things in a first aid kit.Postage stamps: Stamps aren't medical, though Britain's Penny Black of 1840 was the world's first adhesive postage stamp.

Things printed on a business card.Name: A name is the one thing every card carries, and in Japan the card is handed over with both hands and a slight bow.
Things printed on a business card.Job title: A job title tells people what you do, and it often decides how a card is perceived.
Things printed on a business card.Company name: The company name anchors the card, and a card's design is often part of a firm's brand.
Things printed on a business card.Phone number: A phone number is still the classic way to reach someone, though email now rivals it.
Things printed on a business card.Email address: An email address on a card is standard, and many people list a professional one rather than a personal one.
Things printed on a business card.Website: A website gives people a place to learn more, and many cards now include a QR code too.
Things printed on a business card.Company logo: A company logo gives instant recognition, and the standard card size in the US is 3.5 by 2 inches.
Things printed on a business card.Office address: An office address tells people where to find you and often anchors a company's local presence.
Things printed on a business card.Fax number: Fax numbers once appeared on every card, and some still do in industries like law and healthcare, particularly in Japan.
Things printed on a business card.Salary: Salary is private information, so you'd never put it on a card handed to strangers.
Things printed on a business card.Date of birth: A date of birth is sensitive personal data that could be misused, so cards leave it out.
Things printed on a business card.Blood type: Blood type matters in emergencies, but it isn't a business detail, though in Japan people casually link it to personality.
Things printed on a business card.Star sign: A star sign is a personal quirk with no role on a professional card.
Things printed on a business card.Shoe size: Shoe size is irrelevant to business unless you sell shoes.
Things printed on a business card.Hobbies: Hobbies belong in conversation after the handshake, not on a card.
Things printed on a business card.Favorite food: Your favorite food might be a good icebreaker, but it doesn't belong on a card.
Things printed on a business card.Weight: Weight is personal and has no place on a card.
Things printed on a business card.Height: Height is personal data and irrelevant to doing business.
Things printed on a business card.Pet's name: A pet's name might make a cute email password, which is exactly why it shouldn't appear on a card.
Things printed on a business card.Bank details: Bank details are private financial info that you'd hand out only on an invoice.
Things printed on a business card.Passport number: A passport number is a serious identity risk, which is why it never goes on a card.
Things printed on a business card.Credit score: A credit score is confidential financial data and never printed on a card.
Things printed on a business card.Favorite movie: A favorite movie makes conversation on a first date but doesn't help a business card.
Things printed on a business card.Wi-Fi password: A Wi-Fi password is for guests at your office, and printing it on a card would hand it to everyone.

Cardio exercises.Running: Humans are among the best distance runners in the animal kingdom, cooling off by sweating while most animals must stop and pant.
Cardio exercises.Cycling: Riding a bike at a steady pace is gentle on the joints, and a cyclist uses far less energy per mile than a walker.
Cardio exercises.Swimming: Water supports your body weight, so swimming works your heart and muscles while putting very little stress on your joints.
Cardio exercises.Jump rope: Ten minutes of skipping can burn about as many calories as a much longer jog, which is why boxers train with it.
Cardio exercises.Rowing: Rowing is a full-body workout: the legs supply roughly 60 percent of the power in each stroke, not the arms.
Cardio exercises.Jumping jacks: Jumping jacks began as a military drill and spread to gyms and schoolyards; Americans also know them as side-straddle hops.
Cardio exercises.Burpees: The burpee was invented in the 1930s by physiologist Royal H. Burpee as a quick test of fitness, and it has haunted gyms ever since.
Cardio exercises.Zumba: Zumba began in the 1990s when Colombian trainer Beto Perez forgot his aerobics music and improvised with salsa tapes from his bag.
Cardio exercises.Stair climbing: Climbing stairs burns more calories per minute than jogging at a slow pace, and towers host races up thousands of steps.
