Cardio exercises.Sprinting: Sprinting is all-out effort in short bursts, and brief sprint intervals can improve fitness about as much as much longer steady cardio.
Cardio exercises.Kickboxing: Kickboxing blends karate-style kicks with Western boxing punches and became a popular cardio class because a session can burn hundreds of calories.
Cardio exercises.Spinning: Spinning was invented by cyclist Johnny Goldberg in the 1980s to train for a race across America, using indoor bikes.
Cardio exercises.Power walking: Power walking, a brisk pace of around 4 to 5 miles per hour with pumping arms, raises the heart rate enough to count as proper cardio.
Cardio exercises.Deadlift: A heavy deadlift is a strength lift, not cardio, though it recruits more muscle than almost any other exercise.
Cardio exercises.Bench press: The bench press builds the chest, shoulders and triceps in short, heavy sets, which makes it strength work rather than cardio.
Cardio exercises.Bicep curls: Curls isolate a single muscle group with short sets, so they build the arms but do little for your heart and lungs.
Cardio exercises.Static stretching: Holding a stretch improves flexibility but barely raises your heart rate, and research suggests it is best done after a workout.
Cardio exercises.Plank: A plank trains core endurance by holding still; it is muscular work, not cardio, though it feels brutal after one minute.
Cardio exercises.Meditation: Meditation lowers heart rate rather than raising it, which is the opposite of what cardio does.
Cardio exercises.Napping: Napping is the opposite of cardio, though a 20-minute nap is shown to improve alertness more than extra coffee for many people.
Cardio exercises.Foam rolling: Foam rolling massages muscle and fascia, which is recovery work that loosens you up rather than a cardio exercise.
Cardio exercises.Shrugs: Shrugs target the trapezius muscles at the neck and shoulders; they are strength work with weights, not heart-pumping cardio.
Cardio exercises.Wrist curls: Wrist curls train the small forearm muscles, and with so little muscle involved they hardly raise your heart rate.
Cardio exercises.Leg extension: The leg extension machine isolates the quadriceps, a strength move, and is rarely used to get a cardio effect.

Good sources of protein.Chicken: A cooked chicken breast holds roughly 30 grams of protein per 100 grams, making it one of the leanest sources.
Good sources of protein.Eggs: One large egg has about 6 grams of protein, and its protein is a gold standard for how well the body uses it.
Good sources of protein.Lentils: Lentils pack roughly 18 grams of protein per cooked cup, and are among the oldest cultivated crops.
Good sources of protein.Tofu: Tofu is curdled soy milk, and the firmer the block, the more protein per slice.
Good sources of protein.Tuna: Tuna is roughly a quarter protein by weight, which is why canned tuna is a cheap protein source.
Good sources of protein.Beef: Beef supplies all the essential amino acids, plus iron that the body absorbs easily.
Good sources of protein.Greek yogurt: Straining removes the whey, so Greek yogurt carries much more protein than regular yogurt.
Good sources of protein.Chickpeas: Chickpeas offer protein and fiber, and the liquid from canned ones, aquafaba, whips like egg whites.
Good sources of protein.Salmon: Salmon gives protein plus omega-3 fats, and its pink color comes from the pigment astaxanthin.
Good sources of protein.Peanuts: Peanuts have more protein than most nuts, around 7 grams per ounce, because they are really legumes.
Good sources of protein.Turkey: Turkey is high in protein, and the Thanksgiving sleepiness is mostly overeating rather than tryptophan.
Good sources of protein.Cottage cheese: Cottage cheese is rich in casein, a slow-digesting milk protein popular with athletes.
Good sources of protein.Cucumber: Cucumber is about 95 percent water, leaving almost nothing for protein.
Good sources of protein.Apple: An apple has about half a gram of protein, so it is fiber and sugar rather than a protein source.
Good sources of protein.Lettuce: Lettuce is mostly water, with very little protein in a whole head.
Good sources of protein.Celery: Celery is about 95 percent water, famously low in calories and in protein.
Good sources of protein.Rice cake: Puffed rice cakes are mostly starch, with only about 1 gram of protein each.
Good sources of protein.Watermelon: Watermelon is about 92 percent water and has almost no protein.
Good sources of protein.Olive oil: Olive oil is pure fat with zero protein.
Good sources of protein.Sugar: Pure sugar has no protein, only carbohydrate.
Good sources of protein.Honey: Honey contains trace protein, but it is essentially sugar.
Good sources of protein.Grapes: Grapes hold carbohydrates and water, with only about a gram of protein per cup.
Good sources of protein.Orange juice: Orange juice offers vitamin C and sugar, but only about 2 grams of protein per cup.
Good sources of protein.Butter: Butter is about 80 percent fat, and churning removes most of the milk protein.

Symptoms of a common cold.Runny nose: Mucus traps viruses, and its change to yellow or green is just immune cells, not proof of a bacterial infection.
Symptoms of a common cold.Sneezing: A sneeze can send thousands of droplets into the air, which is how colds hop from person to person.
Symptoms of a common cold.Sore throat: A cold's scratchy throat is inflamed tissue and is often the first sign, fading within a few days.
Symptoms of a common cold.Cough: A cough is a reflex clearing the airway, and cold coughs can linger for a couple of weeks.
Symptoms of a common cold.Stuffy nose: A stuffy nose is mostly swollen blood vessels in the nasal lining, not just extra mucus.
Symptoms of a common cold.Watery eyes: Tear ducts drain into the nose, so a swollen nasal lining can back up tears and water the eyes.
Symptoms of a common cold.Congestion: Congestion is swollen nasal tissue, and decongestants work by shrinking those blood vessels.
Symptoms of a common cold.Hoarse voice: A hoarse voice results when inflamed vocal cords can't vibrate smoothly.
Symptoms of a common cold.Headache: Cold headaches often come from sinus pressure behind the face.
Symptoms of a common cold.Postnasal drip: The body makes a quart or so of mucus daily, normally swallowed unnoticed, until a cold makes it noticeable.
Symptoms of a common cold.Broken bone: A fracture is an injury, not an infection, so a cold cannot cause it.
Symptoms of a common cold.Toothache: Sinus pressure can mimic upper tooth pain, but a toothache is not a cold symptom.
Symptoms of a common cold.Sunburn: Sunburn is UV damage to skin, not a sign of illness.
Symptoms of a common cold.Hiccups: Hiccups are diaphragm spasms, not infection; Charles Osborne reportedly hiccupped for about 68 years.
Symptoms of a common cold.Bruise: Bruises are blood leaking under the skin after impact, not a virus at work.
Symptoms of a common cold.Blister: A blister is fluid cushioning damaged skin, from friction or burns.
Symptoms of a common cold.Sprain: A sprain is a stretched or torn ligament, a mechanical injury rather than a cold symptom.
Symptoms of a common cold.Hair loss: Hair loss isn't a cold symptom, though a high fever or illness can shed hair months later.
Symptoms of a common cold.Dandruff: Dandruff is linked to a skin yeast called Malassezia and isn't a cold sign.
Symptoms of a common cold.Freckles: Freckles come from clusters of melanin triggered by sun, not illness.
Symptoms of a common cold.Splinter: A splinter is a tiny foreign object in the skin, unrelated to cold viruses.
Symptoms of a common cold.Ingrown toenail: An ingrown toenail is a nail curling into the skin, with no link to a cold.
Symptoms of a common cold.Shin splints: Shin splints are overuse pain along the shin bone, common among runners.
Symptoms of a common cold.Black eye: A black eye is bruising around the eye from impact, nothing viral.

Things a storybook witch has.Broomstick: The broomstick is the witch's classic ride, and the image comes from medieval tales of witches flying to night gatherings.
Things a storybook witch has.Cauldron: A cauldron is the witch's pot, and in real history it was an everyday cooking pot hung over an open fire.
Things a storybook witch has.Black cat: The black cat became a witch's companion in European folklore, though in Britain a black cat crossing your path is lucky.
Things a storybook witch has.Pointy hat: The pointy hat marks the storybook witch, and some historians link its shape to hats worn by 17th-century Englishwomen.
Things a storybook witch has.Spellbook: A spellbook is where a witch keeps her incantations, and the storybook type is usually dusty, thick, and covered in odd symbols.
Things a storybook witch has.Bubbling potion: A bubbling potion is the witch's brew, and 'double, double toil and trouble' from Macbeth made the cauldron scene famous.
Things a storybook witch has.Black cloak: A black cloak lets a witch vanish into the night, and it's the same black of Halloween costumes now sold worldwide.
Things a storybook witch has.Poison apple: The poison apple from 'Snow White' shows how witches use food, and the story comes from a tale collected by the Brothers Grimm.
Things a storybook witch has.Gingerbread house: A gingerbread house is where witches lure children in 'Hansel and Gretel', a story from the Brothers Grimm in the early 1800s.
Things a storybook witch has.Pet toad: A pet toad is a witch's familiar in old folklore, and some real toads secrete toxins that gave them a creepy reputation.
Things a storybook witch has.Tiara: A tiara belongs to the princess, not the witch, and the word comes from an ancient Persian headdress.
Things a storybook witch has.Glass slipper: The glass slipper is Cinderella's, and some scholars think it began as a mistranslation of a fur slipper in old French.
Things a storybook witch has.Magic carpet: A magic carpet belongs to 'Arabian Nights' tales, not the witch's broom, which is the storybook flight vehicle of Europe.
Things a storybook witch has.Lightsaber: A lightsaber is from Star Wars, a galaxy of science fiction rather than storybook witchcraft and spells.
Things a storybook witch has.Halo: A halo marks angels and saints, which is the opposite of a witch, and the symbol goes back to ancient art.
Things a storybook witch has.Sleigh: A sleigh belongs to Santa, not witches, and his reindeer are drawn pulling it through winter skies.
Things a storybook witch has.Easter basket: An Easter basket belongs to the Easter bunny, a figure that came to America with German immigrants.
Things a storybook witch has.Laser gun: A laser gun is pure science fiction, and real lasers were first made in 1960.
Things a storybook witch has.Surfboard: A surfboard is from the beach, and surfing began centuries ago in Polynesia, far from storybook witches.
Things a storybook witch has.Fire truck: A fire truck has no place in a witch tale, though a cauldron fire might make the witch need one.
Things a storybook witch has.Roller skates: Roller skates are not part of a witch's kit, and the first roller skates were made in the 1700s.
Things a storybook witch has.Hard hat: A hard hat is construction gear, and the first ones were made from canvas and tar for shipyard workers in the early 1900s.
Things a storybook witch has.Tutu: A tutu is a ballerina's tulle skirt, and the classic stiff 'platter' version comes from 19th-century Romantic ballet.
Things a storybook witch has.Unicorn horn: A unicorn horn belongs to a fairy-tale beast, and medieval 'unicorn horns' were really narwhal tusks sold to the rich.

Things a painter-decorator uses.Paint roller: The roller was invented in Canada around 1940 by Norman Breakey, making painting walls much faster.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Paint tray: The ridged slope lets the roller shed excess paint, so each pass lays an even coat.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Drop cloth: Canvas drop cloths absorb paint spills, while plastic sheets are slippery and let drips pool.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Masking tape: Richard Drew of 3M invented it in 1925 after hearing auto painters complain about messy two-tone paint jobs.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Paintbrush: Natural bristle brushes suit oil paints, while synthetic ones are better for water-based paints.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Stepladder: Keeping your belt buckle between the rails is a standard safety tip for stepladder users.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Sandpaper: Chinese craftsmen were gluing crushed shells onto parchment by the 13th century.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Putty knife: Its flexible blade presses filler into holes and cracks and leaves it flush with the wall.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Primer: It seals porous surfaces, so the topcoat looks even and sticks better.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Wallpaper paste: Many pastes are starch-based, which gives a short slip time to adjust the sheet.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Caulk gun: Caulk seals gaps around windows and trim, stopping drafts and moisture.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Easel: An artist's canvas stand; a house painter and an artist both paint, which makes this a tempting trap.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Palette: Artists mix paint on it, while house painters mix in tins; the word comes from the Italian for a little shovel.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Kiln: A potter's oven; porcelain painters use one to fix glaze, not house painters.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Anvil: A blacksmith's heavy block, which would be useless for decorating.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Whisk: It whips air into food, though some painters stir paint with a stick, not a whisk.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Stethoscope: The first stethoscopes were simple wooden tubes in the 1810s.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Plunger: A plumber's suction cup, not a painter's.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Pipe wrench: A plumber's tool with toothed jaws for gripping round pipes.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Telescope: Galileo improved the spyglass in 1609 and turned it toward the sky.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Saddle: A saddle puts a rider on a horse, and stirrups spread widely after steppe peoples used them.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Ladle: A soup scoop, though a painter might use a ladle-like pot to pour paint.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Hoe: A hoe is one of the oldest farm tools, used for weeding and breaking up soil.
Things a painter-decorator uses.Sickle: A curved blade for cutting grain, and it appears on the old Soviet flag.

Railway jobs.Train driver: In the US the job is called a locomotive engineer, and British drivers must learn the routes by heart, a skill called route knowledge.
Railway jobs.Conductor: The conductor runs the train's crew and checks tickets; on a US freight train, the conductor is in charge, over even the engineer.
Railway jobs.Signalman: British signalmen once pulled lever frames in lineside boxes, and a few heritage boxes still run on the Victorian block system.
Railway jobs.Stationmaster: Once a figure of local authority, the stationmaster ran an entire station, and in Britain there was often a grand uniform and a house on site.
Railway jobs.Ticket inspector: Inspectors check passes onboard; in Japan, rail staff are famously punctual and have been known to apologize for departures 20 seconds early.
Railway jobs.Porter: Porters carried luggage, and Pullman porters in the US became a key Black professional group and formed a powerful labor union.
Railway jobs.Track worker: Gangs of track workers once laid rail by hand and the work is still dangerous, often done at night during closed lines.
Railway jobs.Shunter: Shunters couple wagons and move them around yards to make up trains, a job that gave rise to the term shunting.
Railway jobs.Station announcer: Announcers keep passengers informed, and in London the voice of Tube announcements inspired the mind the gap phrase heard daily.
Railway jobs.Pilot: A pilot flies an aircraft, though the same word is used for ship pilots who guide vessels into harbors; neither works on trains.
Railway jobs.Air marshal: Armed officers on flights; the job exists in the sky, not on the rails.
Railway jobs.Flight attendant: Flight attendants work on planes, and the first, Ellen Church in 1930, was a nurse hired to calm passengers.
Railway jobs.Gate agent: This airport job boards passengers at the departure gate, which are airline staff, not railway ones.
Railway jobs.Boatswain: Pronounced bosun, the boatswain looks after the ship's rigging, anchors and deck crew, and the job is among the oldest at sea.
Railway jobs.Deckhand: Deckhands handle lines and cargo on boats, not trains.
Railway jobs.Harbourmaster: The harbourmaster regulates ship traffic in a port, a maritime job without railway ties.
Railway jobs.Ferryman: The ferryman carried people across water, and in Greek myth Charon ferried souls across the river Styx for a coin.
Railway jobs.Coxswain: Called the cox, this person steers a rowing boat and shouts commands to the crew, and traditionally is the lightest person aboard.
Railway jobs.Lifeguard: Lifeguards watch swimmers at pools and beaches, so they have no job on the track.
Railway jobs.Jockey: Jockeys ride horses in races; the railway only shares the word horse in some of its old terms like the iron horse.
Railway jobs.Gondolier: Venice's gondoliers pole through canals, so they'd be at home on a boat and not on rails.
Railway jobs.Shepherd: Shepherds tend flocks, and they sometimes had to wait for a train when railways crossed their pastures.
Railway jobs.Bellhop: A hotel job: the bellhop carries bags for hotel guests rather than at stations.
Railway jobs.Purser: The purser runs the cabin crew and handles money on ships and planes, and the word derives from purse.

Super Mario enemies.Goomba: The first enemy in the first level of Super Mario Bros.; its Japanese name Kuribo means roughly chestnut person.
Super Mario enemies.Koopa Troopa: Walking turtle soldiers whose shells become kickable projectiles once Mario stomps them.
Super Mario enemies.Boo: This shy ghost freezes when you look at it and chases you when you look away; in Japan it's called Teresa.
Super Mario enemies.Bullet Bill: A cannon-fired missile with a face and arms; in Japan its name is simply Killer.
Super Mario enemies.Piranha Plant: In the original game, it won't pop out of its pipe if Mario is standing right on top of the pipe.
Super Mario enemies.Lakitu: A cloud-riding turtle who tosses Spiny eggs, who later became the camera operator in Super Mario 64.
Super Mario enemies.Hammer Bro: A helmeted Koopa who lobs hammers in arcs, and he debuted in the original 1985 Super Mario Bros.
Super Mario enemies.Thwomp: A giant spiked stone that slams down; the name imitates the sound of the thud.
Super Mario enemies.Chain Chomp: Its design reportedly comes from Miyamoto's childhood fear of a neighbor's dog that lunged at him from a chain.
Super Mario enemies.Blooper: A pale squid that lurks in underwater levels, moving in jerky pulses while hunting the swimming Mario.
Super Mario enemies.Shy Guy: The masked, robed creatures first appeared in Doki Doki Panic, which was reworked into Super Mario Bros. 2.
Super Mario enemies.Dry Bones: A skeletal Koopa that collapses when stomped but rebuilds itself seconds later, so stomping never really finishes it.
Super Mario enemies.Cheep Cheep: The fish that swim or leap from the water in Mario's aquatic levels, some jumping out to hit you.
Super Mario enemies.Wiggler: A caterpillar that turns angry and speeds up after being stomped, one of Super Mario World's memorable enemies.
Super Mario enemies.Octorok: A trap: Octoroks are rock-spitting octopus creatures from The Legend of Zelda, not Mario.
Super Mario enemies.Moblin: Pig-faced warriors who have been Zelda enemies since the very first game.
Super Mario enemies.Keese: Bats that flutter through Zelda dungeons. They're from Link's world, not Mario's.
Super Mario enemies.Creeper: Minecraft's green exploding mob, which famously came from a coding mistake while the creator was trying to make a pig.
Super Mario enemies.Ghast: A floating, crying ghost from Minecraft's Nether that shoots fireballs. Not a Mario enemy.
Super Mario enemies.Waddle Dee: Kirby's most common enemy, a round orange creature from Dream Land, so it belongs to Kirby.
Super Mario enemies.Metroid: Floating, jellyfish-like parasites that drain energy; they're the creatures that gave the Metroid series its name.
Super Mario enemies.Headcrab: Half-Life's headgrabbing parasites that turn people into zombies, from Valve's universe, not Mario's.
Super Mario enemies.Bokoblin: The goblin-like enemies with common red variants in Breath of the Wild, so they are from Zelda.
Super Mario enemies.Tonberry: A small lantern-carrying, knife-wielding Final Fantasy monster that slowly stalks the party.

Impressionist painters.Monet: His 1872 harbor scene Impression, Sunrise gave the whole movement its name, when a critic sneered that it was barely finished.
Impressionist painters.Renoir: He painted dancers and café scenes in glowing color, and his figures often feel like candid snapshots of Parisian life.
Impressionist painters.Degas: Though shown with the Impressionists, he preferred indoor scenes of ballet dancers and was a master of unusual, cropped angles.
Impressionist painters.Pissarro: The only artist to show in all eight Impressionist exhibitions, he mentored Cézanne and Gauguin and painted rural life.
Impressionist painters.Sisley: A British-born Frenchman who painted mostly landscapes around the Seine, he died nearly penniless despite his skill with skies.
Impressionist painters.Berthe Morisot: One of the first women in the group, she exhibited in seven of the eight Impressionist shows and painted domestic scenes.
Impressionist painters.Mary Cassatt: An American in Paris, she was invited by Degas to join the group and became famous for tender portraits of mothers and children.
Impressionist painters.Caillebotte: A wealthy heir, he bought his friends' paintings to keep them afloat; his huge Paris Street, Rainy Day is a famous cityscape.
Impressionist painters.Frédéric Bazille: He died at 28 in the Franco-Prussian War, but his friendship and financial help had been a lifeline for Monet and Renoir.
Impressionist painters.Van Gogh: Close, but not Impressionist: his thick brushwork and emotional intensity mark him as Post-Impressionist, who followed after the movement.
Impressionist painters.Toulouse-Lautrec: He chronicled Paris nightlife, but his bold outlines and flat color made him a Post-Impressionist whose posters defined Moulin Rouge.
Impressionist painters.Picasso: He co-founded Cubism and worked in many styles over a seventy-year career, but never the soft, light-chasing look of Impressionism.
Impressionist painters.Matisse: A leader of Fauvism, he used wild, flat color; that bold style came after Impressionism, not as part of it.
Impressionist painters.Salvador Dalí: A Surrealist famed for melting clocks, he was born decades after Impressionism's heyday and belongs to a very different movement.
Impressionist painters.Rembrandt: A Dutch Golden Age master of light and shadow in the 1600s, he predates Impressionism by about two centuries.
Impressionist painters.Vermeer: He painted quiet domestic scenes in 1600s Delft, long before Impressionism; only about three dozen of his paintings survive.
Impressionist painters.Andy Warhol: The Pop Art icon turned soup cans and celebrities into silkscreens in the 1960s, nearly a century after Impressionism.
Impressionist painters.Jackson Pollock: An Abstract Expressionist, he dripped paint onto canvases laid on the floor, a method far from Impressionism's gentle brushstrokes.
Impressionist painters.Gustav Klimt: The Austrian Symbolist behind The Kiss covered canvases with gold leaf; he was Art Nouveau-era, not Impressionist.
Impressionist painters.Edvard Munch: The Norwegian painter of The Scream was an Expressionist, who painted anxiety and emotion instead of fleeting light.
Impressionist painters.Frida Kahlo: Mexican painter famed for vivid self-portraits, she was shaped by her pain and folk art, not by French Impressionism.
Impressionist painters.René Magritte: He painted a man with an apple obscuring his face; Belgian Surrealism, not Impressionism, was his world.
Impressionist painters.Caravaggio: This 1600s Italian used dramatic, theatrical lighting called tenebrism, centuries before the Impressionists painted open air.
Impressionist painters.Michelangelo: A Renaissance giant of sculpture and the Sistine Chapel ceiling, he lived about 350 years before Impressionism began.

Fictional places from books.Narnia: Narnia is entered through a wardrobe in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe, and in it, a lamp-post stands in the woods.
Fictional places from books.Neverland: Neverland is where Peter Pan, Wendy, and the Lost Boys live, and Barrie put a pirate ship there.
Fictional places from books.Oz: Oz first appeared in Baum's 1900 book and has since inspired thirteen sequels by Baum himself.
Fictional places from books.Wonderland: Wonderland is the world Alice finds down the rabbit hole, and Carroll made up the story for a real girl, Alice Liddell.
Fictional places from books.Lilliput: Lilliput is the land of tiny people Gulliver visits in Swift's satire, where political parties differ on how to crack an egg.
Fictional places from books.Hogwarts: Hogwarts is the school of witchcraft and wizardry hidden in the Scottish Highlands in Harry Potter.
Fictional places from books.Middle-earth: Middle-earth is Tolkien's world; the name derives from the Old English middangeard, meaning the world of men.
Fictional places from books.Shangri-La: Shangri-La, from James Hilton's Lost Horizon (1933), is a hidden Himalayan paradise where people age extremely slowly.
Fictional places from books.Brobdingnag: Brobdingnag is the land of giants in Gulliver's Travels, where he is treated like a pet by a farm girl.
Fictional places from books.Discworld: Discworld is Terry Pratchett's flat world, carried on four elephants standing on the back of a giant turtle.
Fictional places from books.Earthsea: Earthsea is Ursula K. Le Guin's archipelago, where magic users must know the true names of things.
Fictional places from books.Panem: Panem is the nation in The Hunger Games, and its name comes from the Latin phrase bread and circuses.
Fictional places from books.Westeros: Westeros is the continent in A Song of Ice and Fire, whose Iron Throne is forged from the swords of conquered enemies.
Fictional places from books.Macondo: Macondo is the village in Gabriel García Márquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude, where magical events seem ordinary.
Fictional places from books.Timbuktu: Timbuktu is a real city in Mali, and it was once famed for its manuscripts and Islamic scholarship.
Fictional places from books.Kathmandu: Kathmandu is the real capital of Nepal, set in a valley below the Himalayas, so it isn't a fictional place.
Fictional places from books.Transylvania: Transylvania is a real region of Romania, though Bram Stoker's Dracula made it feel like fiction.
Fictional places from books.Verona: Verona is a real Italian city, and tourists visit a house with a balcony said to be Juliet's, though it's not Shakespeare's.
Fictional places from books.Elsinore: Elsinore is Hamlet's castle, based on a real one, Kronborg in Helsingør, Denmark, so it's real.
Fictional places from books.Baker Street: Baker Street is a real London road, and 221B was a fictional address that didn't exist in Holmes's day.
Fictional places from books.Sherwood Forest: Sherwood Forest is a real Nottinghamshire woodland, famous for the Major Oak and its link with Robin Hood.
Fictional places from books.Tintagel: Tintagel is a real Cornish castle site; legend says King Arthur was conceived there, but real history is murkier.
Fictional places from books.Zanzibar: Zanzibar is a real island off Tanzania, long a center of the spice and slave trades, and the birthplace of Freddie Mercury.
Fictional places from books.Xanadu: Xanadu was a real place, Kublai Khan's summer capital Shangdu, before Coleridge's poem made it a dream.

Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Robin Hood: Robin Hood is the outlaw of Sherwood who steals from the rich, but the earliest ballads show him as a yeoman, not a nobleman.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Maid Marian: Maid Marian does not appear in the earliest ballads and is added later, becoming a staple by the 16th century.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Friar Tuck: Friar Tuck is the jolly friar of the outlaw band, known for his skill in fighting and for love of food.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Little John: Little John is a huge outlaw, so the name is ironic, and he becomes Robin Hood's right-hand man.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Will Scarlet: Will Scarlet, also called Scarlock, is a member of the band, usually a dashing and hot-tempered young man.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Alan-a-Dale: Alan-a-Dale is the minstrel of Robin Hood's band, who sings of their deeds and weds with their help.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Guy of Gisborne: Guy of Gisborne is a bounty hunter who is hired to catch Robin, and he is killed by him in an early ballad.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Prince John: Prince John is Richard's scheming brother, who rules while the king is away and was later King John, who signed Magna Carta.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.King Richard: King Richard the Lionheart is the crusader king who returns to restore justice, though he spent very little time in England.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.King Arthur: King Arthur is a legendary British king of the Round Table, not part of Robin Hood's tale.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Merlin: Merlin is Arthur's wizard, from a different legend, and not part of Sherwood Forest.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Lancelot: Lancelot is Arthur's greatest knight and Guinevere's lover, from Camelot rather than Sherwood.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Guinevere: Guinevere is Arthur's queen and not part of Robin Hood's legend, which has Maid Marian instead.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Galahad: Galahad is the purest knight of the Round Table, who finds the Holy Grail, in Arthurian legend.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Mordred: Mordred is Arthur's treacherous knight, who is not in Robin Hood's tale.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.William Tell: William Tell is a Swiss archer who shot an apple from his son's head, though a bowman, he's not Robin.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Don Quixote: Don Quixote is Cervantes's Spanish knight who tilts at windmills, with no link to Sherwood.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Sancho Panza: Sancho Panza is Don Quixote's earthy squire, from Cervantes's Spanish novel.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Zorro: Zorro is a masked fencer defending the poor in Spanish California, created in 1919; he's often called a Robin Hood.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.D'Artagnan: D'Artagnan is the young Gascon in The Three Musketeers, based on a real 17th-century French soldier.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Lady Godiva: Lady Godiva, in legend, rode naked through Coventry to protest taxes, which is not part of Robin Hood.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Beowulf: Beowulf is the Old English poem's hero, a monster-slayer, so he's not in Sherwood.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Peter Pan: Peter Pan is J. M. Barrie's boy who never grows up, and he's not a Sherwood outlaw.
Characters in the Robin Hood legend.Rob Roy: Rob Roy was a real Scottish outlaw, Robert Roy MacGregor, nicknamed Scotland's Robin Hood, but he's not English legend.

Written by Agatha Christie.Death on the Nile: Christie set this Poirot case on a Nile steamer after visiting Egypt, and wrote part of it at the Old Cataract Hotel in Aswan.
Written by Agatha Christie.The ABC Murders: A killer sends Poirot letters naming towns in alphabetical order, hiding a single real motive among the apparently random murders.
Written by Agatha Christie.Evil Under the Sun: The seaside hotel is modelled on Burgh Island off Devon, where Christie stayed and wrote.
Written by Agatha Christie.The Mousetrap: This play opened in London in 1952 and is the longest continuously running show in history; audiences are asked not to reveal the ending.
Written by Agatha Christie.Five Little Pigs: Poirot re-examines a sixteen-year-old murder using five accounts of one day, and the title comes from a nursery rhyme.
Written by Agatha Christie.Curtain: Poirot's last case was written in the 1940s and kept in a bank vault for about 30 years; his death made the front page of the New York Times.
Written by Agatha Christie.Peril at End House: Poirot meets a young woman in Cornwall who keeps surviving what look like attempts on her life.
Written by Agatha Christie.Crooked House: Christie named this standalone novel, with no Poirot or Marple, as one of her own favorites; the title comes from a nursery rhyme.
Written by Agatha Christie.Endless Night: A late, darker departure from her usual formula, narrated by a young chauffeur chasing a dream house.
Written by Agatha Christie.Sleeping Murder: Miss Marple's final case was written during World War II but locked away and published only after Christie's death in 1976.
Written by Agatha Christie.Cards on the Table: The murder happens during a bridge game, and Poirot studies the players' scoring sheets for clues to character.
Written by Agatha Christie.Hallowe'en Party: A girl boasts she saw a murder, then drowns in an apple-bobbing tub; Christie dedicated it to P. G. Wodehouse.
Written by Agatha Christie.Towards Zero: Christie's theme is that murder is the end of a long chain, with the story building toward the zero-hour crime.
Written by Agatha Christie.The Big Sleep: Raymond Chandler's 1939 debut introduced Philip Marlowe, and the plot is so tangled that even he reportedly couldn't say who killed the chauffeur.
Written by Agatha Christie.The Maltese Falcon: Dashiell Hammett's detective Sam Spade chases a jeweled bird statuette; the 1941 Humphrey Bogart film made it iconic.

Chewy foods.Gummy bear: Gummy bears were invented in 1922 by Hans Riegel, founder of Haribo, who first made them as dancing bears.
Chewy foods.Taffy: Taffy gets its chew from being pulled over and over, which works air into it and lightens its color.
Chewy foods.Beef jerky: The word jerky comes from the Quechua ch'arki, meaning dried meat, a food the Inca made long before cowboys.
Chewy foods.Bagel: Bagels are boiled before they're baked, which gives them their shiny crust and dense chew.
Chewy foods.Licorice: Real licorice flavor comes from a root containing glycyrrhizin, sweeter than sugar, and eating a lot can raise blood pressure.
Chewy foods.Caramel: Caramel is sugar heated until it browns, a process called caramelization that happens around 170 degrees Celsius.
Chewy foods.Chewing gum: Lumps of chewed birch tar thousands of years old have been found, still carrying tooth marks and even ancient DNA.
Chewy foods.Mochi: Making mochi by pounding steamed rice with giant mallets, a ritual called mochitsuki, is a Japanese New Year tradition.
Chewy foods.Calamari: Calamari turns rubbery when overcooked; cook it very briefly or very slowly, and avoid the middle.
Chewy foods.Tootsie Roll: Tootsie Roll was introduced in 1896 and named for founder Leo Hirshfield's daughter, whose nickname was Tootsie.
Chewy foods.Fruit leather: Fruit leather is puréed fruit dried into a sheet, a way to preserve fruit that has been used for centuries.
Chewy foods.Starburst: Starburst began life in Britain in 1960 as Opal Fruits and took its current name in the 1990s.
Chewy foods.Potato chip: Legend says chef George Crum invented chips in 1853 to spite a customer who wanted thinner fries, though the tale is disputed.
Chewy foods.Cracker: A cracker is supposed to snap, and a chewy one is a stale one, because humidity has crept into it.
Chewy foods.Popcorn: Popcorn pops when water inside the kernel turns to steam around 180 degrees Celsius and bursts the hull.
Chewy foods.Celery: Celery's crunch has fed the myth of negative calories, but it's false: digesting it burns far less than it provides.
Chewy foods.Pudding: Pudding is smooth and needs almost no chewing, and British pudding can mean anything from dessert to sausage.
Chewy foods.Soup: The word restaurant is said to come from a French meat broth sold as a restorative, which makes soup oddly historic.
Chewy foods.Ice cream: Ice cream is churned to keep ice crystals tiny, giving it a smooth melt rather than a chew.
Chewy foods.Yogurt: Yogurt is milk fermented by bacteria, one of the oldest fermented foods, and it needs no chewing at all.
Chewy foods.Cotton candy: Cotton candy dissolves instantly because it's mostly air and spun sugar; a dentist, William Morrison, co-invented the machine.
Chewy foods.Meringue: Baked meringue shatters and melts on the tongue; the marshmallowy chewy center belongs to its cousin, the pavlova.
Chewy foods.Smoothie: A smoothie is blended, so there's nothing to chew; blending breaks open plant cells but keeps the fiber.
Chewy foods.Jell-O: Gelatin makes Jell-O wobble, and gummy bears use it too, but with much less water, which is the difference between wobbly and chewy.

Things that sink in water.Anchor: An anchor holds a ship partly through its weight and partly through the way its flukes dig into the seabed.
Things that sink in water.Coin: Coins sink because the metal is far denser than water, and tossing them into fountains is an old wishing custom.
Things that sink in water.Rock: Most rocks sink, but pumice, formed from frothy lava full of gas bubbles, is a rock that floats.
Things that sink in water.Key: A metal key is several times denser than water, so it sinks fast, which is why keychains often have floating tags.
Things that sink in water.Brick: Bricks sink because they're denser than water, yet they absorb water through tiny pores.
Things that sink in water.Golf ball: A golf ball sinks, and divers recover thousands of lost balls from water hazards each year.
Things that sink in water.Marble: Glass marbles are about two and a half times denser than water, so they sink fast.
Things that sink in water.Iron nail: Iron is about eight times denser than water, though an iron ship floats because its hull encloses lots of air.
Things that sink in water.Fresh egg: A fresh egg sinks and lies flat, but as it ages, air seeps in through the shell and it eventually floats.
Things that sink in water.Potato: Potatoes are denser than water, and the density can reveal their starch content, since a high-starch one sinks faster.
Things that sink in water.Grape: A grape is slightly denser than water and sinks, though it can bob up in fizzy drinks.
Things that sink in water.Metal spoon: A steel spoon sinks, but surface tension lets a very light object, like a needle, rest on water.
Things that sink in water.Apple: Apples float because about a quarter of their volume is air, which is why they're used in bobbing games.
Things that sink in water.Banana: Bananas float since they're less dense than water, and the peel traps lots of air.
Things that sink in water.Ice cube: Ice floats because water expands as it freezes, making ice about 9 percent less dense than liquid water.
Things that sink in water.Cork: Cork floats because it's full of tiny sealed air pockets, and it has been used for fishing floats for ages.
Things that sink in water.Pumpkin: Pumpkins float because they're partly hollow, and there are pumpkin regattas, where people paddle giant ones.
Things that sink in water.Coconut: Coconuts float thanks to air in the husk, which lets them drift across oceans to colonize new islands.
Things that sink in water.Rubber duck: A rubber duck floats because it's hollow, and in 1992, a spill of thousands of them became an ocean-current study.
Things that sink in water.Driftwood: Driftwood floats because wood is less dense than water, and some can drift for years.
Things that sink in water.Pinecone: Pinecones float because their scales trap air, and they close up when wet.
Things that sink in water.Ping-pong ball: A ping-pong ball floats because it's hollow, and is only about 2.7 grams.
Things that sink in water.Tennis ball: A tennis ball floats thanks to its air-filled core, and the felt traps even more air.
Things that sink in water.Watermelon: A watermelon floats, since it's less dense than water, and the fruit is about 92 percent water.

Ford car models.Escort: The Escort was one of the best-selling cars in the world in the 1980s, and was sold in both Europe and America.

Ford car models.Prius: The Prius is Toyota's hybrid pioneer, launched in Japan in 1997 and named for the Latin for 'to go before'.
Ford car models.Accord: The Accord is a Honda, and its Ohio plant in 1982 made it the first Japanese car built in America.

Pieces of a knight's armor.Breastplate: Covers the chest, and later breastplates were proofed by firing a bullet at them; the dent was the maker's guarantee.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Gauntlet: A mailed or plated glove; throwing one down on the ground is the origin of the phrase throw down the gauntlet.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Greaves: Shin armor, from the Old French for a shin guard, which also gave the name to greaves in ancient Greek hoplites.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Chainmail: Thousands of linked rings, each riveted or welded by hand, which made one shirt a very labor-intensive item.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Visor: The movable front of a helmet that covers the face, from Old French vis, meaning face.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Pauldron: Guards the shoulder and upper arm, and the word comes from French espaule, meaning shoulder.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Gorget: Protects the throat, and the word later survived as a small ornamental crescent worn by officers.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Sabatons: Armored shoes, often with long pointed tips that were fashionable in the 1400s, called solerets in the plate version.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Cuirass: From French cuir, meaning leather, though the armor was made of metal, since the first breastplates were leather.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Vambrace: Forearm armor, the plate that sits between the elbow and the wrist and shields the arm from blows.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Doublet: A padded garment often worn beneath armor to cushion blows, so it is clothing that fits the knight, not armor.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Cape: A cloth piece hanging from the shoulders, so it is a garment, not armor.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Sash: A band worn across the body for decoration or rank, so it adds ceremony but no protection.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Ruff: A stiff pleated Elizabethan collar, a fashion item and not armor.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Corset: A corset shapes the waist by lacing, so it's clothing and not armor, though some armor looked similar.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Bonnet: A bonnet is a soft cap tied under the chin, usually worn by women or children, so it's not a piece of armor.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Kilt: A kilt is a Scottish pleated garment, and not armor, though Highland warriors did wear mail.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Toga: A toga is a draped Roman garment, so it's a robe and not armor, and Roman soldiers wore other gear.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Cravat: A cravat is a cloth neckwear, said to be from Croatian soldiers, and it's no armor.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Waistcoat: A waistcoat is a sleeveless garment worn under a jacket, so it's clothing, not armor.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Scabbard: A scabbard is a sheath for a sword, so it is a weapon accessory, not armor.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Lance: A lance is a long spear used by mounted knights in jousts, so it is a weapon, not armor.
Pieces of a knight's armor.Quiver: A quiver holds arrows, which makes it an archer's accessory, not armor.

Bad-luck superstitions.Black cat crossing: In Britain and Japan it's lucky, but in the US it's seen as bad luck. Black cats were once associated with witches.
Bad-luck superstitions.Broken mirror: Said to bring seven years of bad luck. Romans believed life renewed in seven-year cycles and mirrors held part of your soul.
Bad-luck superstitions.Under a ladder: Often traced to the ladder-and-wall triangle, an old symbol of the Trinity, which walking through would violate. Also a practical falling-paint hazard.
Bad-luck superstitions.Umbrella indoors: One theory is that rigid-spoked umbrellas of the early 1800s could poke eyes or knock things over indoors.
Bad-luck superstitions.Friday the 13th: Its fear even has a name, paraskevidekatriaphobia. Some US buildings and airlines still skip the date.
Bad-luck superstitions.Spilling salt: Salt was precious, so wasting it was serious. Tossing a pinch over your left shoulder blinds the devil lurking there. Judas spills it in The Last Supper.
Bad-luck superstitions.Number 13: Many hotels and hospitals skip a 13th floor. In Norse myth the trickster Loki was an uninvited 13th guest.
Bad-luck superstitions.Shoes on the table: Widely held across Europe, with one plain explanation: shoes carry street dirt onto your food. Others link it to death.
Bad-luck superstitions.Macbeth in a theater: Actors call it "the Scottish play" to avoid saying the name backstage. Saying it is said to bring disaster.
Bad-luck superstitions.Four-leaf clover: Only about one in 10,000 clovers has four leaves, which is partly why finding one feels lucky.
Bad-luck superstitions.Horseshoe: It's lucky, hung open-end up to hold the luck in. Iron was also thought to drive off evil spirits.
Bad-luck superstitions.Rabbit's foot: A lucky charm, although it did not help the rabbit. It's strongly tied to folk traditions in the American South.
Bad-luck superstitions.Wishbone: Two people pull it and whoever gets the larger piece gets a wish. The tradition is credited to the Etruscans and Romans.
Bad-luck superstitions.Shooting star: A wish-granting sight, though meteors are mostly specks of dust no bigger than a grain of sand.
Bad-luck superstitions.Ladybug: Lucky: in Europe they protected crops from pests, and their name honors the Virgin Mary, "Our Lady's bug."
Bad-luck superstitions.Lucky penny: Picking one up is supposed to bring luck, though "find a penny, pick it up" doesn't say anything about a penny's real value.
Bad-luck superstitions.Number 7: Lucky in many cultures and a favorite casino symbol: three 7s is the classic slot machine jackpot.
Bad-luck superstitions.Crossed fingers: A gesture to wish luck, though children also cross fingers behind their backs to cancel out a fib.
Bad-luck superstitions.Knocking on wood: Lucky, and tied to old beliefs about friendly tree spirits. Today people knock to avoid tempting fate.
Bad-luck superstitions.Maneki-neko: The Japanese beckoning cat, whose raised paw is said to invite customers and money. Which paw is raised matters.
Bad-luck superstitions.Bird poop on you: In many places, such as Russia and Italy, being hit by bird droppings is considered good luck.
Bad-luck superstitions.Beginner's luck: Luck for newcomers is mostly a trick of memory and small samples, yet most players still swear by it.
Bad-luck superstitions.Wishing well: Tossing a coin in a wishing well is a lucky ritual with ancient roots in offerings to water spirits.
Bad-luck superstitions.Lucky charm: Athletes love them: Michael Jordan reportedly wore his North Carolina shorts under his Bulls uniform.

Things that grant wishes in stories.Fountain coins: Rome's Trevi Fountain collects more than a million euros every year, which is donated to charity.

Things that grant wishes in stories.Magic mirror: The Snow White queen's mirror tells truths and answers questions, but never grants wishes.
Things that grant wishes in stories.Ouija board: Patented as a game in 1890 and sold as a parlor toy. It lets spirits spell out messages, not grant wishes.
Things that grant wishes in stories.Tarot card: Tarot began as a 15th-century Italian card game. Fortune-telling uses came later, and none grant wishes.
Things that grant wishes in stories.Rabbit's foot: A lucky charm, but it only protects, it doesn't grant wishes. Sadly it did little for the rabbit.
Things that grant wishes in stories.Horseshoe: A lucky object, hung open-end up so the luck won't spill out. It protects, but it grants no wishes.
Things that grant wishes in stories.Fortune cookie: The fortune is a prediction, not a granted wish. Despite the name, the cookie probably came from California.

Things that grant wishes in stories.Time-Turner: Hermione's device for going back in time a few hours. It lets her attend more lessons, not make wishes.
Things that grant wishes in stories.Dreamcatcher: Rooted in Ojibwe tradition, it's meant to filter bad dreams from good ones, not to grant any wishes.
Things that grant wishes in stories.Pensieve: Dumbledore's stone basin for viewing stored memories, in Harry Potter. It shows the past, not wishes.
Things that grant wishes in stories.Palantir: One of Tolkien's seeing-stones for viewing faraway places, and not wish-granting. Sauron could corrupt anyone using it.
